Source: https://github.com/Liceron/nexura/blob/main/docs/observability.md

# Observability with OpenTelemetry

Nexura can emit [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) traces for agents, teams and
workflows. Tracing is opt-in: until you call `instrument()`, nothing is imported and nothing
is recorded (the cost is one `None` check). Span and attribute names follow the
[OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai),
pinned to one version (see [Semantic convention version](#semantic-convention-version)).

Install the API package with the extra:

```bash
pip install "nexura-agents[otel]"
```

`instrument()` imports `opentelemetry-api` lazily and raises an `ImportError` that tells you
to install the extra if it is missing. It never sets the global `TracerProvider`: it uses the
provider you pass, or `opentelemetry.trace.get_tracer_provider()`.

The in-house tracer and OTLP JSON export in `nexura_runtime.observability` keep working
unchanged; the two can run side by side.

## Try it in memory

This example runs offline with a fake model and keeps the spans in memory. It needs
`opentelemetry-sdk`, which is a dev dependency of this repository.

```python
from nexura_agents import Agent, FakeModel, Runner, ToolCall, tool
from nexura_agents.tracing import instrument, uninstrument
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter

exporter = InMemorySpanExporter()
provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter))
instrument(tracer_provider=provider)


@tool
def lookup(order_id: str) -> str:
    return f"Order {order_id} shipped."


model = FakeModel(
    responses=[
        [ToolCall(id="c1", name="lookup", arguments={"order_id": "A1"})],
        "Your order shipped.",
    ]
)
agent = Agent(name="Support", instructions="Help.", model=model, tools=[lookup])
Runner().run(agent, "Where is A1?")
uninstrument()

names = sorted(span.name for span in exporter.get_finished_spans())
assert names == [
    "chat FakeModel",
    "chat FakeModel",
    "execute_tool lookup",
    "invoke_agent Support",
]
run = next(s for s in exporter.get_finished_spans() if s.name.startswith("invoke_agent"))
assert run.attributes["nexura.run.status"] == "completed"
```

`uninstrument()` stops new spans; spans already started still finish.

## Export to an OTLP collector

Configure the SDK the way you would for any Python service, then call `instrument()`.

```python notest
from nexura_agents.tracing import instrument
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor

provider = TracerProvider(resource=Resource.create({"service.name": "support-bot"}))
provider.add_span_processor(
    BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint="http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"))
)
instrument(tracer_provider=provider)
```

This needs `pip install opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp`. Spans nest under
whatever span is current when you start a run, so a web framework's request span becomes the
parent of the agent run automatically. The context survives `asyncio.TaskGroup`,
`asyncio.gather` and `asyncio.to_thread`, so parallel tool calls, parallel team members and
parallel workflow branches keep the right parents.

## Semantic convention version

Nexura implements the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, which are still in
**Development** status and now live in their own repository. The version implemented is
pinned to commit
[`8538971bd11dba723fdd33c804b5a32121827ff7`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/tree/8538971bd11dba723fdd33c804b5a32121827ff7)
of `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai` (2026-10-21, schema
`https://opentelemetry.io/schemas/gen-ai-dev/1.42.0-dev`, built on semantic-conventions
v1.44.0). The tracer is created with that schema URL, and
`nexura_agents.tracing.SEMCONV_GENAI_COMMIT` holds the commit. Because the conventions can
still change, a later Nexura release may follow a newer commit; renamed attributes keep a
deprecated alias for one release, as below.

## What is recorded

| Span (kind) | Created for | Key attributes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invoke_agent <agent>` (`INTERNAL`) | Each `Runner` run or resume (including streaming) | `gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_agent`, `gen_ai.agent.name`, `nexura.run_id`, `nexura.run.status` (`completed`, `paused`, `failed`, `cancelled`), `nexura.run.resumed`, `gen_ai.conversation.id` (the `session_id`, when the run has one), `gen_ai.prompt.name` / `gen_ai.prompt.version` (registry prompts), usage totals (`gen_ai.usage.*`) |
| `chat <model>` (`CLIENT`) | Each model call | `gen_ai.operation.name=chat`, `gen_ai.provider.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.response.id` and `gen_ai.response.model` (when the provider reports them), `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` (the conventions' values: `stop`, `length`, `content_filter`, `tool_call`, and `error` when the call failed; Nexura's own `tool_calls` is also kept in `nexura.response.finish_reasons`), `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.cache_write.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens` (cache and reasoning only when reported and non-zero) |
| `execute_tool <tool>` (`INTERNAL`) | Each tool call | `gen_ai.operation.name=execute_tool`, `gen_ai.tool.name`, `gen_ai.tool.call.id`, `nexura.tool.retry_reason` (model retry, rejected), `nexura.tool.pending_approval=true` for a call waiting for approval |
| `invoke_team <team>` (`INTERNAL`) | Each team run or resume | `gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_team` (a custom value), `nexura.team.name`, `nexura.team.kind`, `nexura.team.status`, `nexura.run.resumed`, usage totals |
| `invoke_workflow <spec name>` (`INTERNAL`) | Each `run`, `resume`, `resume_interrupt` and `fork` | `gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_workflow`, `gen_ai.workflow.name`, `nexura.workflow.name`, `nexura.workflow.run_id`, `nexura.workflow.operation`, `nexura.workflow.status`, `nexura.workflow.step_count` |
| `workflow.node <node id>` | Each node step | `nexura.workflow.node.id`, `.step`, `.kind`, `.attempts`, `nexura.workflow.pause_reason` (`approval` or `interrupt`); one `nexura.workflow.retry` event per retried attempt |
| `workflow.branch <name>` / `workflow.map_item <index>` | Each parallel branch or map item | `nexura.workflow.branch`, `nexura.workflow.map_index` |

Span names follow the conventions' `{gen_ai.operation.name} {name}` format.
`gen_ai.provider.name` uses the conventions' well-known values: `anthropic`, `gcp.gemini`
(the Gemini API), `gcp.vertex_ai` (`nexura-vertex`), the provider prefix of a LiteLLM model
string (`bedrock/...` is `aws.bedrock`, no prefix is `openai`), and the custom values
`sarvam` and `fake` (the test models). The OpenAI chat and Responses adapters and
`OpenAIChatModel` are named by their base URL: `api.openai.com` is `openai`,
`*.openai.azure.com` is `azure.ai.openai`, and the hosted OpenAI-compatible APIs of Groq,
DeepSeek, Mistral, xAI, Perplexity, Moonshot and Gemini get their own values. Any other
endpoint (a local Ollama or vLLM server, a proxy) gets no value. A custom model can declare
its own with a `gen_ai_provider_name` string attribute. When the provider is unknown the
attribute is left out rather than guessed, although the conventions make it Required on
inference spans and metrics: the attribute is a discriminator for provider-specific
telemetry, and a made-up value would be wrong for every consumer that relies on it. Retry,
rate-limit and fallback wrappers report the provider of the (first) model they wrap. Response ids and models come from non-streamed responses of the
OpenAI chat and Responses, Anthropic, Gemini (`responseId`, `modelVersion`), Sarvam and
LiteLLM adapters; they are absent for streamed calls.

Why teams keep `invoke_team`: the conventions list crew-style orchestration
(`Crew.kickoff()`) as an `invoke_workflow` example, so a team could be reported as a
workflow. Changing it renames every team span and its metrics, so it is kept as a custom
operation value in this release; `gen_ai.workflow.name` is not set on team spans.

Nesting: `invoke_team` > `invoke_agent` > `chat` / `execute_tool`; `invoke_workflow` >
`workflow.node` > branch or item, a sub-workflow's own `invoke_workflow` span, or an agent
run started by the node's handler. An agent used as a tool nests under the `execute_tool`
span.

Errors set the span status to `ERROR`, add an `exception` event and set `error.type` (the
exception class name, for example `RuntimeError` on a `chat` span whose provider call failed
and `ProviderError` on its run span). Exception text can echo credentials or user data, so with `capture_content` off (the default) only the exception type is recorded (status description, `exception.type`, `error.type`); with `capture_content=True` a redacted, truncated message is added as `exception.message` and the status description. Run metadata attributes (`nexura.run.metadata.*`) drop secret-named keys and redact string values, like `span()` attributes. `RUN_FAILED` run events are not spans and still carry the exception text. Two things
are deliberately not errors: an approval pause (the run, tool and node spans end normally
with `paused` status or `pending_approval`), and a `ModelRetry`, which is a request to the
model rather than a failure. A resumed run is a new span with the same `nexura.run_id`.

## Approvals, budgets, durable effects and guardrails (`nexura.*` events)

Four things the GenAI conventions do not cover are recorded as span events in the
`nexura.*` namespace. They carry ids, counts, classes and statuses only: never arguments,
results, reasons, actors or other content, whatever `capture_content` says.

| Event | Recorded on | Attributes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nexura.approval.requested` | The `invoke_agent` span of a run that pauses for approval (also a reapproval and an `effect_unknown` pause after a crash); the `workflow.node` span of a gated node; the current span for a node's `request_approval()` | `nexura.approval.id` (interruption or approval id), `nexura.approval.kind` (`tool_call` or `workflow_node`), `nexura.approval.reason` (`approval`, `effect_unknown`, `node_request`), `nexura.approval.pending_count` and `nexura.approval.tools` (tool names), `nexura.workflow.node.id` |
| `nexura.approval.decided` | The resumed `invoke_agent` span, once the approval is consumed: right after the decision checks, or, with a journal-capable checkpoint store, after the resumed run has recorded its claim in the journal and consumed the approval. A wrong digest, an expired or already spent approval records nothing, and each approval records it once: when a resume stopped after its journal claim but before consuming the approval, `recover()` consumes it and records the event on the recovered run's span; when the stopped resume had already consumed it, recovery adds none. The `invoke_workflow` span of a workflow resume | `nexura.approval.id`, `nexura.approval.kind`, `nexura.approval.decision` (`approve`, `reject`, `mixed` or `answer`), `nexura.approval.approved_count`, `.rejected_count`, `.answered_count`, `.resolved_count` (agents), `nexura.approval.inputs_edited` (workflows) |
| `nexura.budget.reserve` | The current span (the `chat` span for non-streamed model calls) | `nexura.budget.model`, `nexura.budget.method` (`generate`, `stream`, `embed`), `nexura.budget.reservation_id`, `nexura.budget.estimated_tokens` |
| `nexura.budget.settle` | Same | `nexura.budget.model`, `nexura.budget.reservation_id`, `nexura.budget.outcome` (`settled`, or `released` for a failed or never-dispatched call), `nexura.budget.input_tokens`, `nexura.budget.output_tokens` |
| `nexura.budget.refuse` | Same | `nexura.budget.model`, `nexura.budget.method`, `nexura.budget.estimated_tokens`, `nexura.budget.limit_type` (when the budget reports one), `error.type` (for example `BudgetExceededError`) |
| `nexura.effect.intent` | The `invoke_agent` span of a durable run (journal-capable checkpoint store); the current workflow span for workflows | `nexura.effect.id`, `nexura.effect.step_key`, `nexura.effect.class` (`non_idempotent`, `idempotent`, `reconcilable`, `pure`), `nexura.effect.status=pending`, `nexura.run_id`, `nexura.approval.id` (when the step runs under an approval) |
| `nexura.effect.outcome` | Same | Same, with `nexura.effect.status=confirmed` |
| `nexura.effect.unknown` | Same | Same, with `nexura.effect.status=indeterminate` (a timed-out call, a crash, a failed run with dispatched steps) |
| `nexura.effect.resolved` | Same | Same, with `nexura.effect.resolution` when a resolution is committed through the journal |
| `nexura.guardrail.decision` | The `invoke_agent` span for an agent input or output guardrail; the `execute_tool` span for a tool guardrail. Recorded for every outcome other than a pass, together with a `GUARDRAIL_DECISION` run event holding the same fields (see [Guardrail decision events](guardrails-hooks-limits.md#guardrail-decision-events)) | `nexura.guardrail.stage` (`input`, `output`, `tool_input`, `tool_output`), `nexura.guardrail.check` (the guardrail's name), `nexura.guardrail.action` (`fail`, `scrub`, `reject`), `nexura.guardrail.latency_ms`, `nexura.guardrail.source` (`live`), `gen_ai.tool.name` and `gen_ai.tool.call.id` on tool stages, `error.type` for a guardrail that crashed or timed out; from the guardrail's `info`, only when they are short tokens or plain values: `nexura.guardrail.categories`, `.score`, `.backend`, `.cached`, `.rule`, `.decision` |

The budget events are recorded once per budget that reserves. Nested run budgets of one
hierarchy are combined into the deepest scope, which records one event; independent
allowances (for example a run budget and a separate per-model allowance) each record their
own. When no span is open at that moment (for
example a streamed model call, whose admission happens while the stream is read), the event
is exported as a zero-length span with the same name and attributes, so it is not lost. These
helpers never raise and do nothing while tracing is off or OpenTelemetry is not installed.

## Your own spans and grouped traces

`tracing.span(name, **attributes)` wraps your own code in a span nested under whatever is
current: inside a tool it nests under that tool call, in your application under your own
spans. `tracing.trace(name, group_id=..., metadata=...)` puts every run started inside the
block under one parent span, so a batch job or a multi-step request shows as one trace;
`group_id` (`nexura.trace.group_id`) links separate traces, such as the turns of one
conversation. Both do nothing while tracing is off.

```python
import asyncio

from nexura_agents import Agent, FakeModel, Runner, ToolCall, tool, tracing
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter

memory = InMemorySpanExporter()
provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(memory))
tracing.instrument(tracer_provider=provider)


@tool
def report(region: str) -> str:
    """Build a sales report."""
    with tracing.span("query warehouse", region=region) as step:
        step.set("rows", 120)
    return "120 rows"


model = FakeModel(
    responses=[[ToolCall(id="c1", name="report", arguments={"region": "west"})], "Done."]
)
agent = Agent(name="Reports", instructions="Use tools.", model=model, tools=[report])

with tracing.trace("nightly reports", group_id="2026-10-11", metadata={"team": "sales"}):
    asyncio.run(Runner().run_async(agent, "west region"))
tracing.uninstrument()

names = [s.name for s in memory.get_finished_spans()]
assert "query warehouse" in names and "trace nightly reports" in names
```

Attribute values must be strings, numbers or booleans. Other values and secret-named keys
(`api_key`, `password`, ...) are dropped, and strings go through the same credential
redaction as captured content. An exception inside the block marks the span as failed and
is re-raised. Custom spans record no duration metric.

## Metrics

`instrument()` also records the metrics of the GenAI conventions. They use the meter from
`meter_provider=` (default: the global `MeterProvider`, which does nothing until you
configure the OpenTelemetry SDK), and the global provider is never set.

| Metric | Type, unit | Recorded for | Attributes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gen_ai.client.inference.duration` | Histogram, `s` | Each model call | `gen_ai.operation.name=chat`, `gen_ai.provider.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.response.model`, `error.type` when it failed |
| `gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration` | Histogram, `s` | Each agent run | `gen_ai.agent.name`, `error.type` |
| `gen_ai.execute_tool.duration` | Histogram, `s` | Each tool call | `gen_ai.tool.name`, `error.type` |
| `gen_ai.invoke_workflow.duration` | Histogram, `s` | Each workflow run | `gen_ai.workflow.name`, `error.type` |
| `gen_ai.client.inference.usage.input_tokens`, `.output_tokens`, `.cache_read.input_tokens`, `.cache_write.input_tokens`, `.reasoning.output_tokens` | Counter, `{token}` | Each model call that reports the count | The inference attributes above and `gen_ai.token.modality=unknown` (providers do not report a per-modality split to Nexura) |
| `gen_ai.client.inference.operation.input_tokens`, `.output_tokens` | Histogram, `{token}` | Each model call that reports usage | The inference attributes above |
| `gen_ai.client.token.usage` (deprecated) | Histogram, `{token}` | As before 0.4.0: each model call that reports usage, once per `gen_ai.token.type` | `gen_ai.token.type`, `gen_ai.operation.name=chat`, `gen_ai.request.model` |
| `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` (deprecated for model calls) | Histogram, `s` | As before 0.4.0: each agent run, model call, tool call, team run and workflow run | `gen_ai.operation.name` with the pre-0.4.0 values (`workflow` for workflows, not `invoke_workflow`), plus `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.agent.name`, `gen_ai.tool.name`, `nexura.team.name` or `nexura.workflow.name`, and `error.type` (`cancelled` for a cancelled run or tool call) |

Bucket boundaries are the ones the conventions recommend for each histogram. Metric
attributes are low-cardinality on purpose: no run ids, call or response ids, tags or
content. Tokens are counted only on model calls, so the totals add up without double
counting the run and team spans. Handoff marks and tool calls waiting for approval are not
timed. Team runs are timed only in `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` (there is no
convention metric for a custom operation). A run or workflow that pauses for approval and is
resumed records one duration point per segment (each span), not one end-to-end value; a
workflow resume that only records a rejection records no `gen_ai.invoke_workflow.duration`
point. A model call that fails before a response records
no token counts. Pass `instrument(metrics=False)` to record spans only.

```python
import asyncio

from nexura_agents import Agent, FakeModel, Runner, Usage
from nexura_agents.tracing import instrument, uninstrument
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import InMemoryMetricReader
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider

reader = InMemoryMetricReader()
instrument(tracer_provider=TracerProvider(), meter_provider=MeterProvider(metric_readers=[reader]))
agent = Agent(
    name="Support",
    instructions="Be brief.",
    model=FakeModel(responses=["hi"], default_usage=Usage(12, 3, 15)),
)
asyncio.run(Runner().run_async(agent, "hello"))
uninstrument()

data = reader.get_metrics_data()
names = {m.name for rm in data.resource_metrics for sm in rm.scope_metrics for m in sm.metrics}
assert {
    "gen_ai.client.inference.duration",
    "gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration",
    "gen_ai.client.inference.usage.input_tokens",
    "gen_ai.client.inference.usage.output_tokens",
} <= names
```

To export, configure a `MeterProvider` with an OTLP metric exporter
(`opentelemetry-exporter-otlp`) the same way as the tracer provider above.

## Privacy: `capture_content`

By default no instructions, prompts, completions, tool arguments or results, or workflow
state are recorded; spans carry only names, ids, counts, statuses and token usage. Pass
`instrument(capture_content=True)` to add them. Content is recorded as span attributes in
the structured format of the GenAI conventions' JSON schemas, serialized to a JSON string
(OpenTelemetry Python span attributes cannot hold structured values yet):

| Attribute | On | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gen_ai.system_instructions` | `chat` | The agent's instructions (the leading system messages), as `[{"type": "text", "content": ...}]` |
| `gen_ai.input.messages` | `chat` | The chat history sent to the model: `[{"role", "parts": [...]}]` with `text`, `tool_call` (`id`, `name`, `arguments`), `tool_call_response` (`id`, `response`), `uri` and `blob` parts. Inline attachment bytes are never copied (`blob` content is a size placeholder). |
| `gen_ai.output.messages` | `chat` | The model's reply, one message. Its finish reason is in `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` (always recorded, also with capture off), not in the message: the pinned schema deprecates `finish_reason` on output messages |
| `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` | `execute_tool` | Tool arguments (JSON object) |
| `gen_ai.tool.call.result` | `execute_tool` | The tool result (parsed as JSON when it is JSON text, otherwise the text) |

Other content is recorded as span events:

| Event | Attribute | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gen_ai.content.prompt` (deprecated) | `gen_ai.prompt` | Messages sent to the model (on `chat`) |
| `gen_ai.content.completion` (deprecated) | `gen_ai.completion` | The model's reply (on `chat`) |
| `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` (deprecated) | `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` | Tool arguments (on `execute_tool`) |
| `gen_ai.tool.call.result` (deprecated) | `gen_ai.tool.call.result` | Tool result text (on `execute_tool`) |
| `nexura.workflow.input` / `nexura.workflow.output` | `nexura.workflow.state`, `nexura.workflow.update` | Workflow state at start and end, and each node's update |
| `nexura.handoff.reason` | `nexura.handoff.reason` | The model's handoff reason, or its structured `input_type` arguments (on `handoff A -> B`) |

Every value is passed through credential redaction (secret-named fields in any spelling such as `accessToken` or `Set-Cookie`, bearer and basic
credentials, `key=value` credentials, provider API keys). Event values are truncated to 4000
characters; in the structured attributes each text value is truncated to 4000 characters
(the JSON stays valid). `gen_ai.input.messages` holds at most the newest 100 messages of
the history, and the oldest of those are dropped when the value would pass 64,000
characters, so the current turn is always kept. Inside one value, lists and objects keep
their first 100 items and nesting stops at 12 levels (`"[DEPTH LIMIT]"`). Attachment URLs
lose their query string, user name and fragment (`https://host/path?...`, presigned URLs
carry their signature there); only `http`, `https` and `gs` URLs are kept, any other scheme
(such as a `data:` URL, which holds the bytes themselves) is replaced by a placeholder; and
inline attachment bytes are replaced by a size marker,
in the attributes and in the deprecated events. A tool result is parsed as JSON only when it
is at most 64,000 characters long; otherwise, or if it cannot be parsed, it is recorded as
text. Content that cannot be converted at all is left out: recording content never changes
or fails a run. Redaction is
best effort and is not a personal-data detector: names, addresses and other personal data
in prompts are recorded as written. Turn content capture on only where your trace backend is
allowed to hold that data.

## Deprecated aliases

These names changed when Nexura moved to the pinned conventions in 0.4.0. The old names are
still emitted next to the new ones for one release and are **removed in 0.5.0**
(`nexura_agents.tracing.ALIASES_REMOVED_IN`). Move dashboards and queries to the new names.

| Old (deprecated) | New | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gen_ai.system` | `gen_ai.provider.name` | `chat` spans (same value) |
| `nexura.usage.reasoning_tokens` | `gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens` | `chat`, run and team spans |
| `gen_ai.operation.name=workflow`, span `workflow <name>` | `gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_workflow`, span `invoke_workflow <name>`; the old value stays in `nexura.operation.name=workflow` | Workflow spans (the span name itself changed in 0.4.0) |
| Events `gen_ai.content.prompt` / `gen_ai.content.completion` | Attributes `gen_ai.input.messages` (with `gen_ai.system_instructions`) / `gen_ai.output.messages` | `chat` spans, with `capture_content=True` |
| Events `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` / `gen_ai.tool.call.result` (not names the conventions define) | Attributes `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` / `gen_ai.tool.call.result` | `execute_tool` spans, with `capture_content=True` |
| `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons=["tool_calls"]` | `["tool_call"]` (the conventions' value); the raw value stays in `nexura.response.finish_reasons` | `chat` spans |
| Metric `gen_ai.client.token.usage` (`gen_ai.token.type`) | `gen_ai.client.inference.usage.input_tokens` / `.output_tokens` counters and the `gen_ai.client.inference.operation.*_tokens` histograms | Model calls |
| Metric `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` for model calls, agent runs, tool calls and workflows | `gen_ai.client.inference.duration`, `gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration`, `gen_ai.execute_tool.duration`, `gen_ai.invoke_workflow.duration` | Recorded exactly as before 0.4.0, including `gen_ai.operation.name=workflow` for workflows. From 0.5.0 it is no longer recorded for model calls (the conventions reserve it for non-inference operations) and workflows use `invoke_workflow` |

The Nexura V2 trace exporter forwards `gen_ai.provider.name` and still reads `gen_ai.system`
from spans recorded by older instrumentation.

Source: https://github.com/Liceron/nexura/blob/main/docs/templates.md

# Starter templates

Nexura ships a catalog of starter workflows. Each one is a versioned JSON file, validates
against the workflow engine, and has a test fixture that runs it end to end offline, with no
network and no model provider. The same tests run in CI for every template.

| Template id | Category | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `support-desk-refund-approval` | support | Classify a message; a refund waits for a human approval before it is issued. |
| `rag-qa-citations` | knowledge | Answer from the documents you supply with numbered citations; refuse when nothing matches. |
| `research-team` | agents | Planner, researcher, writer and reviewer agents in sequence. |
| `approval-workflow` | governance | Small requests pass; large ones pause for approve or reject. |
| `scheduled-report` | automation | Collect, summarise and queue a report; ships a suggested weekly schedule. |
| `structured-extraction` | data | Free text to a typed invoice record; incomplete documents are flagged, not guessed. |

## What "offline" means here

The handlers behind the templates (`tpl_*`, in `nexura_runtime.templates.handlers`) are
deterministic stand-ins. Steps that stand for an LLM call run a real `Agent` on a scripted
`FakeModel`. Steps that stand for an outside system (a payment API, a mail server) only record
what they would do: the refund is `simulated`, and the report goes to a dry-run outbox
(`sent: false`). A template is therefore a runnable, tested skeleton of the flow and its
approval gates. To go live, register your own handlers or modules and point the instantiated
workflow's nodes at them.

`required_credentials` lists, by name only, what a live version needs (for example
`model_api_key`). The offline template does not use them. They are never stored in a template.

## File format

Each file in `src/nexura_runtime/templates/data/<id>.json` has:

- `template_version` (currently `1`), `id` (equal to the file name), `title`, `description`,
  `category`, `difficulty` (`beginner`, `intermediate` or `advanced`), `tags`.
- `required_modules`: the handler names the spec uses (checked against the spec on load).
- `required_credentials`: credential names.
- `spec`: a normal workflow spec.
- `suggested_trigger` (optional): a schedule you can attach with the triggers API.
- `sample_input`: state that runs the template.
- `fixture.runs`: test cases with `input`, an optional `approval` (`approve` or `reject` at a
  node), `expect_status`, `expect_state` (dotted paths), `expect_contains`, `expect_absent` and
  `expect_path`.

A file that is malformed, whose spec does not validate, or whose `required_modules` do not
match the spec raises `TemplateError` when the catalog loads.

## Run a template in Python

```python
import asyncio

from nexura_runtime.templates import get_template, list_templates, run_fixture

print([t.id for t in list_templates(category="support")])

template = get_template("approval-workflow")
assert template is not None
outcomes = asyncio.run(run_fixture(template))
for outcome in outcomes:
    assert outcome.failures == [], outcome.failures
    print(outcome.name, "->", outcome.status)
```

## REST API

| Method and path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/v1/templates?category=&tag=` | List the catalog (metadata, `categories` and `tags` facets). |
| `GET /api/v1/templates/{id}` | One template with `spec`, a Mermaid `mermaid` diagram and `sample_input`. |
| `POST /api/v1/templates/{id}/instantiate` | Create a workflow from it. Body: optional `name`, `workflow_id`. |

Instantiating follows the rules of `POST /api/v1/workflows`: viewers get `403`, the full
create-time validation and approval policy apply, and the new workflow belongs to the caller's
workspace only. An unknown template is `404 TEMPLATE_NOT_FOUND`. The response is:

```json
{
  "workflow_id": "wf-...",
  "workflow": {},
  "template_id": "research-team",
  "template_version": 1,
  "missing_credentials": ["model_api_key", "search_api_key"],
  "runs_offline": true,
  "suggested_trigger": null
}
```

`missing_credentials` names the credentials the workspace does not hold; nothing is filled in
for you. The suggested trigger is returned but not created.

## Studio

Open **Templates** in the sidebar (or "Browse the template gallery" in Create Workflow). Filter by
category, tag or search text, preview a template's graph read-only, then choose **Use template**
to create the workflow in the current workspace.

## Adding a template

Add `data/<id>.json` with a fixture, add any new `tpl_*` handler to
`nexura_runtime.templates.handlers`, and run `uv run pytest tests/test_templates.py`. The new
file is picked up and tested automatically.

# Service and Studio

The MIT open-source edition is **single user, this machine only; for a team or a public endpoint use the hosted or enterprise edition**. This holds when you embed the service too: `create_api_app()` answers 403 `NON_LOOPBACK_CLIENT` to any peer that is not loopback unless you give the explicit insecure opt-in, even under `uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0")`. The one exception is [remote single-operator mode](remote-single-operator.md) (`nexura-runtime serve --auth token`): the same single owner on a remote host or VM, with one operator token on every request, behind a TLS reverse proxy. It adds no accounts or roles.

The platform package `nexura-runtime` includes a local REST service and a browser Studio. The service stores workflows and runs in a SQLite file and exposes them under `/api/v1`. Studio is a React app that talks to that API, and `@liceron/nexura-sdk` is a TypeScript client for the same API. All three are optional: the Python SDK works on its own, and a workflow behaves the same whichever way you start it. Both packages are alpha and unpublished, so install from a source checkout.

## One `nexura` command

The runtime declares `nexura.commands` entry points for `serve`, `worker`, `workflow`,
`repro`, `redteam`, `evals`, `sandbox`, `dev` and `project` (`nexura project init|dev|deploy`,
because `init` and `deploy` are the client's own commands; see
[Project templates](project-templates.md)); the `nexura-studio` package declares `studio`.
Once the Nexura Cloud client supports this group, `nexura serve` and the other
subcommands work through that single command. Until then, use `nexura-runtime`
(or `nexura-studio` for Studio).

## Try the API without a server

You can call the service in-process with `httpx.ASGITransport`, so there is no port and no network. This needs the `studio` extra (FastAPI). A new database is seeded with a demo workflow, `wf-order-support`, which pauses for approval on a refund order.

```python
import asyncio
import os
import tempfile

import httpx

from nexura_runtime.service.api.app import create_api_app


async def main() -> None:
    db = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "service.sqlite3")
    app = create_api_app(db_path=db, profile="local-owner")
    transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=app)
    # Loopback base URL; state-changing requests carry the per-session token (see below).
    session = {"X-Nexura-Session": app.state.session_token}
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        transport=transport, base_url="http://127.0.0.1", headers=session
    ) as client:
        caps = (await client.get("/api/v1/capabilities")).json()
        assert caps["active_profile"] == "local-owner"
        assert caps["supported_profiles"] == ["local-owner"]

        listing = (await client.get("/api/v1/workflows")).json()
        assert "wf-order-support" in [w["workflow_id"] for w in listing["items"]]

        started = await client.post(
            "/api/v1/runs",
            json={
                "workflow_id": "wf-order-support",
                "initial_state": {"order_id": "ORD-DELHI-501"},
            },
        )
        run = started.json()
        assert run["status"] == "pending_approval"

        decision = {"approval_id": run["pending_approval"]["approval_id"], "decision": "approve"}
        decided = await client.post(f"/api/v1/runs/{run['run_id']}/decide", json=decision)
        assert decided.json()["status"] == "completed"

        # An approval can be used once: a second decision is a conflict.
        again = await client.post(f"/api/v1/runs/{run['run_id']}/decide", json=decision)
        assert again.status_code == 409
        assert again.json()["detail"]["code"] == "NOT_PENDING_APPROVAL"


asyncio.run(main())
```

## Run the service

```bash
uv sync --extra studio
uv run nexura-runtime serve --port 8765 --db ./nexura_service.sqlite3
```

The command is `nexura-runtime` (installed by `nexura-runtime`). The bare `nexura` command
belongs to the separate Nexura Cloud client package `nexura`, so this project does not install
a command with that name.

`nexura-runtime serve` takes `--host` (default `127.0.0.1`), `--port` (default `8765`), `--db` (default `./nexura_service.sqlite3`), `--workflow-state-url` (a `postgresql://` URI that keeps workflow checkpoints and their execution journal in Postgres instead of the `--db` file; also `NEXURA_WORKFLOW_STATE_URL`; needs `nexura-postgres`, see [Workflows on Postgres](durable-execution.md#workflows-on-postgres-s8)) and `--worker`, which also runs scheduled and webhook jobs (see [Schedules and webhooks](#schedules-and-webhooks)). It starts the `local-owner` profile: one user, no login. Keep it on `127.0.0.1`; do not expose this profile on a network. The open-source edition has one principal, the local owner (role `admin`): no logins, user accounts, API keys or workspace members, and `X-Principal-*` headers are ignored. Started on a non-loopback address without authentication, the service refuses to start unless you pass the explicit insecure opt-in. To use the service from another machine as its only operator, start it with `--auth token` (an operator token from `NEXURA_OPERATOR_TOKEN` or `--token-file`; `--insecure-plain-http` for a non-loopback bind without a local TLS proxy), see [Run Nexura on a server (single operator)](remote-single-operator.md). A shared multi-user service needs the Nexura enterprise edition. If `nexura-runtime serve` prints that it needs the `studio` extra, install it as shown above.

### Per-session token

Every request other than GET, HEAD and OPTIONS must send the server's per-session token in the `X-Nexura-Session` header; without it the answer is 403 `SESSION_TOKEN_REQUIRED` (or `SESSION_TOKEN_INVALID` for a wrong or old value). This stops a web page in your browser, including one served by another local tool on another port, from changing anything. `nexura-runtime serve` and `nexura-studio` generate a new random token at every start; set `NEXURA_STUDIO_TOKEN` before starting to use a fixed one.

- Studio reads the token from `GET /api/v1/local-session` on its own origin and sends it for you. The server refuses that read when the browser marks it cross-site or same-site (`Sec-Fetch-Site`) or when its `Origin` is another server. The built-in Studio page (`nexura-studio`) also receives it in the page itself; with `NEXURA_STUDIO_TOKEN` set and a non-local browser (Docker), open the page as `http://127.0.0.1:8765/#token=<your token>`.
- The TypeScript client (`@liceron/nexura-sdk`) and the Python `NexuraClient` read the token from that endpoint when the server refuses a request for it, then retry once; pass `sessionToken` / `session_token` to set it yourself.
- Scripts on this machine can read it the same way (`curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/local-session`). An app that embeds `create_api_app()` finds it on `app.state.session_token`.
- State-changing requests must be JSON: `text/plain`, form and multipart bodies are answered with 415. Raw Python source sent to `/api/v1/workflows/import/python` with `Content-Type: text/plain` by a non-browser client is still accepted. Signed webhook deliveries (`/api/v1/triggers/webhooks/{id}/deliver`) need no token.

`GET /api/v1/capabilities` reports `supported_profiles: ["local-owner"]` in OSS. The shared profile requires an installed authenticating provider from the hosted or enterprise edition; selecting its name alone fails closed.

Requests can carry an `X-Workspace-ID` header to choose a workspace. Errors come back as JSON with a `detail` object that has a `code` and a `message`.

The service covers these areas under `/api/v1`:

| Area | Paths |
|---|---|
| Workflows | `/workflows` (list, create, get, update, delete, validate, export, import) |
| Runs | `/runs` (start, get, list, cancel, decide an approval, `/{run_id}/input`, `/{run_id}/history`, `/{run_id}/fork`, `/{run_id}/subruns`, `/{run_id}/effects`, `/events` as server-sent events, `/{run_id}/diagnostics`) |
| Chat sessions | `/sessions`, `/sessions/{id}/chat`, and `/sessions/{id}/chat/stream` for streamed turns |
| Modules and capabilities | `/modules`, `/capabilities` |
| Knowledge | `/knowledge/collections`, `/documents`, `/retrieve`, `/answer` |
| Credentials | `/credentials` (create, list, get, delete, `/verify`, `/revoke`) |
| Integrations | `/integrations` (MCP and OpenAPI discover and test-run, register) |
| Evaluations | `/evaluations` (datasets, runs, compare) |
| Triggers | `/triggers` (schedules, webhooks, jobs, outbox) |
| Workspaces | `/workspaces` |

Saving a workflow that someone else changed first returns HTTP 409 with code `REVISION_CONFLICT`, so you can reload or save a copy. Chat streaming sends ordered events for each model turn and tool call, then the same body as the non-streaming endpoint. Reply text arrives whole, not token by token, and a turn that is cancelled or disconnected is not saved. The chat endpoints answer with a local deterministic `FakeModel`, not a real model, so the playground needs no keys and shows no live model output. The playground also has a `knowledge_search` tool over the caller's workspace knowledge, so answers about your documents carry real citation footnotes (see [Knowledge](knowledge.md)).

## Run Studio

Studio lives in `studio-web/`. It is a private app served by Vite, not a published package.

```bash
cd studio-web
npm ci
npm run dev
```

The dev server proxies `/api` to `http://127.0.0.1:8765`. If your service is elsewhere, set `VITE_BACKEND_URL`. If Studio shows "Unable to connect", the service is not running or that variable points at the wrong place.

Today Studio has these sections: workflows (a graph builder with undo history, validation, import and export, sub-workflow nodes through the composite inspector), templates (the starter workflows), approvals (an inbox for pending approvals and a decision dialog), runs (a timeline, a state replayer and diagnostics, fed by the event stream), a chat playground, modules, knowledge, credentials, tools (MCP and OpenAPI integrations), evaluations (evals and benchmarks), triggers, run traces (a span tree per run), onboarding and system status. The interface is available in English and Hindi.

In the builder, "+ Add Step" opens the module drawer. Its categories follow the module kinds that `GET /api/v1/modules` reports: channels are the `nexura.channel.*` modules, Connectors are the 15 `nexura.connectors.*` integrations, and Tools & APIs holds tools plus the other integrations (HTTP, SQL, speech, MCP). A descriptor with `"internal": true` is a service-internal module (`nexura.service.triggers`, `nexura.observability`, `nexura.evaluation.runner`, `nexura.runtime.approvals`). The drawer does not offer these as new steps. They stay registered, so saved workflows that use them still validate and run. A module sets the flag with `ModuleManifest(internal=True)`. The flag is not part of the manifest digest. The sidebar badge on Approvals shows the number of runs waiting for a decision. It refreshes every 30 seconds while Studio is connected and the tab is visible.

Every run has its own page at `#/runs/{run_id}`: the full Run Console (approve or reject, answer an input request, history and fork, sub-runs, diagnostics, trace, Save as test) and a link back to its workflow. It works after a reload and for runs started by a trigger, the API or another local process. An unknown run, or one from another workspace, shows a notice instead. A run opened on a workflow page is kept in the URL as `#/workflows/{workflow_id}/runs/{run_id}`, so a reload reopens it in the Run Console tab. The workflow page has a Runs tab: the workflow's runs, newest first, 20 per page, with a status filter (`running`, `pending_approval`, `waiting_for_input`, `completed`, `failed`, `rejected`, `cancelled`, `interrupted`). "Open run" links lead to the run page from that tab, the run traces list and trace page, Approvals inbox items, trigger jobs that have a `run_id`, and workflow-test and eval case results saved from a run (`metadata.source_run_id`). The Approvals inbox also has a "Waiting for input" section that lists runs with status `waiting_for_input`; you answer on the run page. The sidebar badge still counts approvals only. The run traces list filters by the same statuses and pages 50 runs at a time.

In the triggers view, the schedule and webhook forms pick the target workflow from the workspace's workflows. There is no free-text workflow id and no default id; a workspace without workflows says so and the forms cannot be submitted. The Triggers button on a workflow page opens `#/triggers/{workflow_id}`: the triggers view lists only that workflow's schedules and webhooks (with a link back to all triggers), and both forms start with that workflow selected. After a webhook is registered, Studio shows the signing secret once, with a Copy button, the delivery URL (`POST /api/v1/triggers/webhooks/{endpoint_id}/deliver`), the three headers (`X-Webhook-Timestamp`, `X-Webhook-Event-ID`, `X-Webhook-Signature`) and curl and Python snippets that sign with the v2 scheme described under [Schedules and webhooks](#schedules-and-webhooks). The secret is kept only in the page's memory. Studio does not write it to local or session storage, the URL or the console, and it is gone after you dismiss the panel, leave the triggers view or switch workspace. The service never returns it again, so if it is lost, delete the webhook and register it again. The snippets read the secret from the `NEXURA_WEBHOOK_SECRET` environment variable and do not contain it, so each webhook card keeps showing its delivery URL and a "How to sign deliveries" section after the secret is dismissed.  The test endpoint picker and the signing section follow the workflow filter: opened from a workflow page they offer only that workflow's webhooks. "Show all triggers" lifts the filter without leaving the view, so a secret still on screen stays there. A workflow id in `#/triggers/{workflow_id}` that is not in the workspace's (complete) workflow list is neither offered nor preselected. The delivery URL is built from the address Studio uses for the service. Under `npm run dev` that is the Vite origin, which proxies `/api` to the service. A sender outside your machine needs an address that reaches the service itself.

There is also an older built-in Studio, started with `uv run nexura-studio --db ./studio.sqlite3` (it defaults to port 8000). It is the separate `nexura-studio` package (`pip install nexura-studio`; the repository's development environment installs it), which also ships its static web page. The REST service needs only the runtime's `studio` extra. New work goes to the REST service and `studio-web`.

## TypeScript client

`clients/typescript` is `@liceron/nexura-sdk`, an HTTP client with no runtime of its own. Build it with `npm install && npm run build` in that directory. Its default `baseUrl` is `http://127.0.0.1:8765`, the port `nexura-runtime serve` uses.

```typescript
import { NexuraClient } from "@liceron/nexura-sdk";

const client = new NexuraClient({ baseUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:8765" });

const run = await client.runs.start({
  workflow_id: "wf-order-support",
  initial_state: { order_id: "ORD-DELHI-501" },
});

if (run.status === "pending_approval" && run.pending_approval) {
  await client.runs.decide(run.run_id, {
    approval_id: run.pending_approval.approval_id,
    decision: "approve",
  });
}
```

The client has `workflows`, `runs`, `modules`, `capabilities`, `workspaces`, `sessions`, `knowledge`, `credentials`, `integrations`, `evaluations` (including `evaluations.studio`), `triggers`, `agents`, `skills`, `templates` and `builder`. It covers only the routes the open-source service serves: clients for the closed edition's hosted routes (organisations, publishing, the hosted secrets admin API and workspace members) ship with the closed edition, for TypeScript and Python alike. `runs.streamEvents()` and `sessions.chatStream()` are async generators for the event streams. An error response throws `NexuraApiError` with `statusCode`, `code` and `details`. A request validation error (FastAPI's 422 list) has code `VALIDATION_ERROR`, a `field: message` text and the original list in `details`. `workspaceId` is sent as `X-Workspace-ID`. The optional `apiKey` client setting is for a hosted or enterprise server; it adds no authentication to OSS.

## Interrupts, history, forks and sub-runs

A handler that calls `interrupt()` pauses the run with status `waiting_for_input`. The run record carries `pending_input`, which is `{"interrupt_id", "node_id", "value"}`. This is different from `pending_approval`, which is only set for approval gates.

```bash
# Start a run; if a handler calls interrupt() the response has status "waiting_for_input".
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/runs \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"workflow_id": "wf-draft-review", "initial_state": {"draft": "Hello"}}'

# Answer it. The value can be any JSON; the run continues and may pause again.
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/runs/RUN_ID/input \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"interrupt_id": "INTERRUPT_ID", "value": {"approved": true}}'

# Every saved checkpoint of the run, oldest first (state is redacted for credential keys).
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/runs/RUN_ID/history

# Start a NEW run from checkpoint 1 with a changed state; returns 201 and the new run.
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/runs/RUN_ID/fork \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"checkpoint_index": 1, "state_update": {"bonus": 10}}'

# Latest checkpoint of each child run started by sub-workflow nodes.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/runs/RUN_ID/subruns
# One child run (key from the list above): status, steps, redacted history.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/runs/RUN_ID/subruns/CHILD_KEY
```

- `POST /runs/{run_id}/input` needs the `approve` permission, like `/decide`. It returns `409 NOT_WAITING_FOR_INPUT` if the run is not waiting, `404 INTERRUPT_NOT_FOUND` for a different interrupt id, and `409 ALREADY_ANSWERED` if another caller answered first. The answer is recorded as an `INPUT_PROVIDED` event with credential-like fields redacted.
- `GET /runs/{run_id}/history` returns `{"items": [checkpoint, ...]}`. A checkpoint has `state`, `current_node_id`, `step_count`, `status`, `interrupt` and `forked_from`.
- `POST /runs/{run_id}/fork` needs the `run` permission and runs synchronously. The new run belongs to the caller's workspace and its record has `forked_from`. The source run is not changed. A bad or out-of-range `checkpoint_index`, or the final checkpoint of a run, returns `400`; a run of another workspace returns `403 CROSS_WORKSPACE_ACCESS_DENIED` (an unknown run `404`); a checkpoint from a different workflow spec returns `409`. Approval gates after the fork point ask again.
- `GET /runs/{run_id}/subruns` returns `{"items": [...]}`: the latest checkpoint of every child run whose id starts with `<run_id>/`, in natural id order (numbers inside an id compare as numbers, so `[2]` comes before `[10]`). It takes `limit` (default 50, 1 to 200) and `offset` and also returns `total`, `limit`, `offset` and `has_more`, like `GET /runs`. A run without sub-workflows returns an empty list. An unknown `child_key` is `404 RUN_NOT_FOUND` naming the key.
- `GET /runs/{run_id}/trace` returns a span tree for the run: `run_id`, `status`, `include_content`, `truncated`, `span_count`, `duration_ms` and a flat `spans` list linked by `parent_id` (a root `run` span, one `node` span per workflow node attempt with status, timing, tokens, cost, model and module, and child spans for model calls, tool calls, retries and handoffs inside agent nodes). The only query parameter is `include_content` (default `false`); inputs, outputs and errors are included, redacted, only when it is `true`, and are always dropped for runs older than the diagnostic retention window. An unknown run returns `404 RUN_NOT_FOUND`. Studio shows it under Run Traces.
- All of these return `403 CROSS_WORKSPACE_ACCESS_DENIED` for a run owned by another workspace and `404 RUN_NOT_FOUND` for an unknown run.
- `GET /runs/{run_id}/effects` returns `{"effects": [...]}`: the run's journaled external effects (`effect_id`, `intent` with its `idempotency_key` and `effect_class`, `status` `pending`/`confirmed`/`indeterminate`/`resolved`, `resolution`, `result` with credential-like fields redacted, `resolved_by`). Only executors that write the execution journal record effects (the service's workflow runs, and `DurableExecutionEngine` sharing the service database); other runs return an empty list. `POST /runs/{run_id}/effects/{effect_id}/resolve` with `{"resolution": "confirmed" | "not_applied" | "failed", "result": ...}` settles an `indeterminate` effect once. It needs the `approve` permission and records the authenticated caller as `resolved_by` (the body cannot name an actor). It returns `409 EFFECT_ALREADY_RESOLVED` the second time, `409 EFFECT_NOT_INDETERMINATE` for another status, `409 RUN_LEASE_HELD` while a worker holds the run and `409 RUN_FINISHED` for a finished run; an unknown effect is `404 EFFECT_NOT_FOUND`. Resolving runs nothing: continue the run with `POST /runs/{run_id}/recover`. A journaled run is looked up in the caller's workspace, so another workspace's run is `404 RUN_NOT_FOUND`. See [Durable execution](durable-execution.md).
- `POST /runs/{run_id}/recover` (optional body `{"on_uncertain": "pause" | "fail"}`, `run` permission) continues a run whose process stopped (`interrupted`) or a `paused` run whose unknown effect was resolved, through `WorkflowEngine.recover`. A step that dispatched without a recorded outcome runs again only if it is `pure` or `idempotent` (same idempotency key) or a `reconcilable` probe says it did not happen; otherwise the run becomes `paused` with `pause_reason: "effect_unknown"` and `pending_effect` (run fields), and you resolve it as above. Refusals: `409 RUN_LEASE_HELD` while a live process executes it, `409 RUN_WAITING_FOR_PERSON` for a run waiting for an approval or an answer, `409 RUN_ALREADY_TERMINAL`, `409 RUN_NOT_JOURNALED` for a run without an execution journal (fork it instead) and `409 SPEC_MISMATCH`. See [Durable execution: the service on the journal](durable-execution.md#the-service-on-the-journal-s9).

The TypeScript client has matching methods:

```typescript
const waiting = await client.runs.start({ workflow_id: "wf-draft-review" });
if (waiting.status === "waiting_for_input" && waiting.pending_input) {
  const done = await client.runs.provideInput(
    waiting.run_id,
    waiting.pending_input.interrupt_id,
    { approved: true },
  );
  const { items } = await client.runs.history(done.run_id);
  const fork = await client.runs.fork(done.run_id, {
    checkpointIndex: 1,
    stateUpdate: { bonus: 10 },
  });
  const children = await client.runs.subruns(done.run_id);
}
```

## Schedules and webhooks

Schedules and signed webhooks enqueue durable trigger jobs. A trigger worker turns each job into a normal workflow run: same engine, approval policy, workspace ownership and events as `POST /runs`, with the schedule payload or webhook body as the initial state. The run is owned by the job's workspace and started by the principal `trigger:<schedule|webhook>:<id>`. Without a worker, jobs stay `pending` and nothing runs.

Start the worker inside the service, or as separate processes that share the same SQLite file. Claims are atomic, so `nexura-runtime serve --worker` and any number of `nexura-runtime worker` processes can run together and each job runs once. With `--workflow-state-url postgresql://...` (or `NEXURA_WORKFLOW_STATE_URL`) the job queue, webhooks and schedules live in Postgres next to the workflow state (`nexura_postgres.PostgresTriggerStore`); webhook secrets are then encrypted with `NEXURA_TRIGGER_SECRET_KEY`, or else the `<database>.trigger.key` file. Studio run records stay in the SQLite file, so processes sharing a Postgres queue must also share that file (one machine) for now.

```bash
nexura-runtime serve --db ./nexura_service.sqlite3 --worker --poll-interval 1
# or, in another terminal (add --once to process due jobs and exit):
nexura-runtime worker --db ./nexura_service.sqlite3 --poll-interval 1
```

A workflow run the service starts is journaled (see [Durable execution: the service on the journal](durable-execution.md#the-service-on-the-journal-s9)): the process executing it holds a run lease and renews it every 10 seconds (`create_api_app(workflow_lease_ttl=30.0)`). Such a run is shown `interrupted` only when its lease is gone: it expired, or its owner was a process on this machine that has exited. The service checks when it starts, when a run is read and when runs are listed, on SQLite and on Postgres workflow state. A run another live `serve` or `worker` executes, on this machine or another, is never shown `interrupted`. Continue an interrupted run with `POST /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/recover` (Python `client.runs.recover(run_id)`, TypeScript `client.runs.recover(runId)`): a step that may have run but must not repeat pauses the run (`status` `paused`, `pause_reason` `effect_unknown`) until you resolve its effect. The rest of this paragraph describes runs recorded before this change (legacy rows): each run in `running` records the process executing it (host name, process id and the process start time). When a `serve` or `worker` process opens the database it marks a legacy `running` run `interrupted` ("Run was interrupted by server restart or shutdown.") only if that process is on the same machine and has exited. A process id reused by a newer process, or one from before a reboot, counts as exited. Runs of a process that is still alive are left alone, so starting a worker, or restarting `serve` while a worker runs, does not interrupt another process's runs. Runs recorded by a database from before this change have no owner and are still marked `interrupted` on open. Runs owned by another machine are never marked, so share a SQLite file between processes on one machine only. On systems without `/proc` the check is weaker: macOS checks only the process id, so a reused process id keeps a dead run in `running`, and Windows treats every owning process as alive, so runs there are marked `interrupted` only by a clean shutdown. A service that shuts down cleanly still marks its own unfinished runs `interrupted` ("Run was interrupted by server shutdown."), unless another worker holds a journaled run's lease by then.

Create a schedule that fires every 60 seconds (`cron_expr` with `timezone` also works). `release_id` pins what may run: `current` (default, no pin), a revision such as `rev:3`, or the workflow's spec hash. If the workflow has changed since, the job fails with a clear error and no run starts. Jobs whose workflow is missing or belongs to another workspace fail the same way.

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/triggers/schedules \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"schedule_id": "nightly", "workflow_id": "wf-123", "interval_seconds": 60,
       "payload": {"msg": "hello from the schedule"}}'
```

Register a webhook, then sign and deliver an event. Webhooks registered through the API use signature scheme v2: HMAC-SHA256, hex encoded, over `v2.<integer unix timestamp>.<event id>.` followed by the canonical JSON body (keys sorted, separators `,` and `:`, no spaces). The event id is part of the signed string, so a captured delivery cannot be replayed under a different `X-Webhook-Event-ID`. Event ids are 1-200 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_:-]` (no dots). The legacy v1 signature (`v1.<timestamp>.<body>`, no event id) is rejected for API-registered endpoints; it is only still accepted for endpoints that existed before v2 and for direct `TriggerManager` use. Deliveries older than the replay window (300 seconds by default) are rejected, and a repeated `(endpoint, X-Webhook-Event-ID)` pair is accepted but creates no second job; ids are scoped per endpoint. The body must be a JSON object. The signing secret is returned only when the webhook is registered and is stored encrypted at rest (key from `NEXURA_TRIGGER_SECRET_KEY`, or a 0600 `<database>.trigger.key` file next to the database). An endpoint id or schedule id already used by another workspace returns 409. Registering a webhook requires the `edit` and `run` permissions, deleting and scheduling require `edit`, and `POST /webhooks/{id}/test` requires `admin` and does not return the computed signature. The signature, replay window and body limit (1 MB) apply in every profile. `openssl -hmac` and `curl -H` put the secret on the command line, where other local users can see them in the process list; on a shared machine sign with the Python snippet instead. Schedule `interval_seconds` must be at least 60 by default (set `NEXURA_MIN_SCHEDULE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` to change it). In [remote single-operator mode](remote-single-operator.md#webhooks) a delivery also needs the endpoint's own delivery token as `Authorization: Bearer` (returned once at registration, rotated with `POST /api/v1/triggers/webhooks/{id}/delivery-credential`), v1 signatures are refused, and every refused delivery is the same 401.

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/triggers/webhooks \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"endpoint_id": "orders", "workflow_id": "wf-123", "secret": "change-me"}'

TS=$(date +%s)
BODY='{"msg":"hello from a webhook"}'   # already canonical: sorted keys, no spaces
EID=evt-0001
SIG=$(printf 'v2.%s.%s.%s' "$TS" "$EID" "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac 'change-me' | awk '{print $NF}')

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1/triggers/webhooks/orders/deliver \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-Webhook-Timestamp: $TS" \
  -H "X-Webhook-Event-ID: $EID" \
  -H "X-Webhook-Signature: $SIG" \
  -d "$BODY"
```


`GET /api/v1/triggers/jobs` lists pending and claimed jobs. After a worker has processed a job it records `status` (`completed` or `failed`), `error_message` and `run_id`. A run that pauses for approval or input counts as a started job: the job is `completed` and the run is `pending_approval` or `waiting_for_input`. A run that ends `failed` marks the job `failed` and keeps its `run_id`. Local limits: the worker uses the handlers registered in its own process, so pass `--handlers package.module:attr` to `nexura-runtime worker` for custom handlers.


### Job leases and crash recovery

A claimed job carries a lease: `lease_expires_at = claimed_at + lease_seconds` (default 300, set with `TriggerWorker(lease_seconds=...)` or `nexura-runtime worker --lease-seconds`). While a run executes, the worker renews the lease every `lease_seconds / 3` and stops when the run finishes. If a worker dies hard (SIGKILL, power loss), its lease expires. At the start of each `run_once`, any worker reclaims expired jobs with an atomic compare-and-swap (SQLite `UPDATE ... WHERE` on the observed owner and lease; Postgres rows locked `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, timed by the database clock; a lock in the memory store), so two workers racing on the same job produce exactly one new owner. This job lease only coordinates the queue: the run's own lease in the execution journal decides who executes the run (see [Durable execution: trigger jobs on the journal](durable-execution.md#trigger-jobs-on-the-journal-s10)).

A job owns one run for its whole life. A reclaimed job (up to `max_attempts` claims in total, default 3, `--max-attempts`; the counter is the persisted `attempts` field) continues that run instead of starting a new one:

- a run that already `completed` is not run again; the job is `completed`. A `failed`, `rejected` or `cancelled` run fails the job with the run's error;
- a run waiting for a person (`pending_approval`, `waiting_for_input`, or `paused` with `pause_reason` `effect_unknown`) counts as started: the job is `completed`;
- a `running` or `interrupted` run whose run lease is gone is continued with `WorkflowEngine.recover` (the same step as `POST /runs/{run_id}/recover`): completed steps do not run again, a step declared `pure` or `idempotent` that may have run is run again (an `idempotent` one with the same idempotency key), and an undeclared (`non_idempotent`) one pauses the run `effect_unknown` until you resolve its effect; the event `RUN_RECOVERY_STARTED` names the job and attempt;
- while another live process still holds the run lease, the worker waits for that run instead of starting anything;
- a run without an execution journal (recorded before this change, or killed before its first journal write) is marked `interrupted` and the job starts a new run; the old id moves to the deprecated `previous_run_ids`.

When the attempts are used up the job becomes `failed` with `worker lease expired N times` and keeps its run, which is marked `interrupted` once its run lease is gone and can still be recovered over the API. A worker that loses its job lease (for example after a long stall) cancels its local run and can no longer complete or fail the job; the worker that took the job over continues the run.

`TriggerWorker(retry_mode="new_run")` (or `nexura-runtime worker --retry-mode new_run`) keeps the behaviour from before: the old run is marked `interrupted` and a NEW run starts from the beginning of the workflow, so side effects that ran before the crash may run again. It is deprecated (it raises a `DeprecationWarning`) and will be removed in 0.6.

Each claimed job runs as its own asyncio task, at most `--max-concurrent-jobs` at a time (default 4), so a long run does not delay schedule ticks or lease recovery. On shutdown the worker waits a grace period (default 20 seconds) for running jobs, then cancels them; a cancelled job is failed with `worker cancelled`. Databases created before leases are migrated by adding nullable columns on open; an old `claimed` job without a lease is treated as expiring one lease period after `claimed_at`, so it is recovered rather than stuck. `nexura-runtime serve --worker` uses the default lease settings.

## Using a real model in chat

The Studio playground and `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/chat` (and `/chat/stream`) use the offline
`fake-deterministic` fixture by default. The operator can allow real models; clients then pick one
by name.

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...          # keys come ONLY from the server environment
nexura-runtime serve --chat-model gpt=openai:gpt-4o-mini --chat-model gem=gemini:gemini-2.5-flash
# or: NEXURA_CHAT_MODELS="gpt=openai:gpt-4o-mini,gem=gemini:gemini-2.5-flash" nexura-runtime serve
```

- `--chat-model NAME=PROVIDER:MODEL` is repeatable; `NEXURA_CHAT_MODELS` holds the same entries
  comma-separated. A CLI entry overrides an environment entry with the same name.
  `PROVIDER:MODEL` is the same string `infer_model` accepts (`openai`, `anthropic`, `gemini`,
  `vertex`, `sarvam`, `ollama`, `litellm`). Programmatic use:
  `create_api_app(chat_models={"gpt": "openai:gpt-4o-mini"}, chat_usage_limits=UsageLimits(...))`
  (values may also be model objects).
- Why an allowlist: requests carry only a configured name (`"model": "gpt"`). Any other value is
  rejected with `400 MODEL_NOT_AVAILABLE` listing the allowed names, so callers cannot choose
  arbitrary providers, endpoints or keys, and no key is ever read from a request.
- Models are resolved lazily on first use. If the key or dependency is missing, only that model
  fails, with `503 MODEL_UNAVAILABLE` (the message never includes key material); the offline
  fixture keeps working.
- `GET /api/v1/chat/models` returns `[{name, provider, label, offline, streaming, default}]`
  (no secrets, no model ids). `fake-deterministic` is always listed and is the default.
- Real models get the playground agent's instructions and tools. Each turn is capped by
  `chat_usage_limits` (default: 10 model requests and 50,000 total tokens per request; exceeding
  it returns `429 USAGE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`). Usage is what the model reports; unknown stays `null`.
- The response `model` is `"<name> (<provider>)"`. `delivery` is `"streamed"` for `/chat/stream`
  when the model produced text deltas, otherwise `"final_only"`.
- Live use calls a paid provider: it is not covered by the test suite, which uses injected fake
  models only. Try it manually from a shell with your own key.

## Describe a workflow

In Studio, **New Workflow** has a **Describe it** button. Type what you want, for example "a support agent that looks up orders and asks a manager before refunds over 100", and press **Draft**. You get an explanation, a list of things to review and a read-only drawing of the draft graph. The draft is marked unsaved: nothing has been saved or run. Press **Create from draft** to save it through the normal validate-then-create path and open it on the canvas, where you edit it like any other workflow, or **Discard draft** to throw it away.

The assistant calls **your** model, with your provider key. It never uses a key of ours:

- Add a provider credential (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini or Sarvam) in Credentials. The draft endpoint uses the workspace's first active provider credential, or the one you name with `credential` (and `model`, to choose the model name).
- On the local service, an operator-configured chat model can be named with `model_ref`. The offline `fake-deterministic` fixture cannot draft.
- With no usable model, `POST /api/v1/builder/draft` returns `400 NO_MODEL_CREDENTIAL`.

```
POST /api/v1/builder/draft
{"description": "...", "credential": "my_openai", "model": "gpt-4o-mini"}
```

The response holds `spec`, `explanation`, `warnings`, `attempts`, `saved: false` and the engine's `validation` report. It follows workflow creation's local-owner and workspace-scoping rules. The description is limited to 4000 characters (`422 DESCRIPTION_TOO_LONG`) and each workspace gets 10 drafts a minute (`429` with `Retry-After`).

What makes the draft trustworthy:

- **The real engine checks it.** The draft goes through the same validation as `POST /workflows/validate`. If it fails, the errors are sent back to the model and it tries again, up to `max_attempts` (default 3, at most 5).
- **Only installed modules.** The model is shown the catalog of installed modules (with schemas) and the template list as examples. A module that is not installed is never accepted: the draft fails with `422 UNKNOWN_MODULES` and a warning naming it. If the registry has a handler called `unconfigured_step`, the step is replaced by it instead.
- **Approvals are enforced in code, and unknown means write.** Any step whose module can write (`idempotent_write` or `non_idempotent_write`), whose effect is unknown, or that the server requires approval for, gets `requires_approval` even if the model, or an instruction hidden in the description, said otherwise. A module with a manifest is judged by its `effect_policy`. A plain handler with no manifest counts as unknown (so it is gated whatever its name) unless you declare it safe by setting `effect_policy = "pure"` (or `"read"`) on the handler function before registering it. Only the handlers shipped with the built-in templates are judged by name. If you ask for sign-off and no step has a gate, a warning says so.
- **The description is data.** It is delimited, cannot close its own delimiter, and text in it that looks like a secret is removed before the model sees it.
- **Bounded prompts.** The catalog lists at most 150 modules, ranked by how well they match your description, followed by "and K more modules not shown". A retry replays at most 4000 characters of the model's previous reply, and each attempt's messages stay under 90,000 characters. A reply that is nested too deeply to parse counts as an unusable reply and is retried.
- **No secrets in the spec.** Every free-form step field (`config`, `input_mapping`, `output_mapping`) is scrubbed. A secret-named key loses its whole value whatever its type, and secret-shaped text anywhere inside is redacted, each with a warning. Reference a credential by name with the config key `credential`.

From Python, with a model you control. This example uses a scripted offline model:

```python
import asyncio
import json

from nexura_agents.models.fake import FakeModel

from nexura_runtime.builder_assistant import draft_from_description
from nexura_runtime.templates import list_templates, template_registry

reply = {
    "explanation": "Classify the message, then refund after approval.",
    "spec": {
        "name": "Refund desk",
        "entry_node": "classify",
        "nodes": [
            {
                "id": "classify",
                "handler": "tpl_support_classify",
                "transitions": {"refund": "refund"},
                "default_transition": "answer",
            },
            {"id": "refund", "handler": "tpl_support_issue_refund", "default_transition": "answer"},
            {"id": "answer", "handler": "tpl_support_reply"},
        ],
        "terminal_nodes": ["answer"],
    },
}
model = FakeModel([json.dumps(reply)])
draft = asyncio.run(
    draft_from_description(
        "support agent that asks a manager before refunds",
        model=model,
        registry=template_registry(),
        templates=list_templates(),
    )
)
print(draft.spec["nodes"]["refund"]["requires_approval"])  # True: refunds write, so they are gated
```

The Sub-runs tab appears only for runs whose workflow has sub-workflow steps (`GET /runs/{run_id}` returns `has_subworkflows`, derived from the spec; the spec itself is not returned), and each child row opens a child view with its status and checkpoint timeline and a link back to the parent run. Child runs are checkpoints inside the parent, so they are read through the parent: `GET /runs/{run_id}/subruns` lists them with an opaque URL-safe `child_key`, and `GET /runs/{run_id}/subruns/{child_key}` returns that child's `status`, `steps` and redacted `history`. A child is visible to whoever can see the parent; an unknown key is `404 RUN_NOT_FOUND`. Studio's graph builder can add and edit sub-workflow (composite) nodes. The same operations remain available over the HTTP endpoints above, the TypeScript client and the Python SDK. See [Workflows](workflows.md).
