## Editions

The open-source edition is MIT: **single user, this machine only; for a team or a
public endpoint use the hosted or enterprise edition**. Local workspaces are project
folders for that one owner, not tenant or member accounts. Loopback binding, Host/Origin
checks, local credentials, approvals, budgets and sandbox safety stay in this edition.
"This machine only" also holds when you embed the service: `create_api_app()` refuses
peers that are not loopback, and state-changing requests need a per-session token
(`X-Nexura-Session`, see [Service and Studio](studio-and-service.md)).
The token stops other web pages, not other programs on this machine, which can read it.
An insecure network opt-in does not add authentication or make a public endpoint safe.
[Remote single-operator mode](remote-single-operator.md) does add authentication (one
operator token, every request; per-endpoint delivery tokens for webhook senders) for that one
owner; it is not multi-user.

The closed edition adds authentication, workspace members, organisations and invites,
managed secrets and rotation, publishing and the embeddable widget, and hosted-product
runtime compatibility. It has not had an external security review. Installing the MIT
packages alone does not enable those features.

## Run the service and Studio web

```bash
uv run nexura-runtime serve --port 8765 --db ./nexura_service.sqlite3   # REST API
cd studio-web && npm ci && npm run dev                                  # Studio on Vite
```

Studio's dev server proxies `/api` to `http://127.0.0.1:8765` (override with
`VITE_BACKEND_URL`). The service defaults to the single-owner `local-owner`
profile and binds to `127.0.0.1`; do not expose it on a network as is.

Schedules and webhooks only enqueue jobs; a worker runs them. Start one with
`nexura-runtime serve --worker` or a standalone `nexura-runtime worker --db ... [--once]`. Claimed jobs
hold a lease the worker renews (`--lease-seconds`, default 300); if a worker dies, the
job is reclaimed (up to `--max-attempts` claims) and continues the run it owns, which is
never run again once it completed. Release pins are enforced and several workers never
double-fire a schedule.

Chat in the service and Studio is offline by default. An operator can allow real models
with `nexura-runtime serve --chat-model NAME=PROVIDER:MODEL` (or `NEXURA_CHAT_MODELS`); API keys
come from the server's environment only, clients choose from `GET /api/v1/chat/models`
and cannot pass provider strings, and viewers can use only the offline fixture. Studio's
playground has a model picker for this.

Runs that wait for a person are visible in the API: a run waiting on `interrupt()` has
status `waiting_for_input` and `pending_input`; `POST /api/v1/runs/{id}/input` answers it,
`GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/history` lists checkpoints, `POST .../fork` starts a new run from
one (optionally with edited state) and `GET .../subruns` lists sub-workflow runs. The TS
client has `runs.provideInput/history/fork/subruns/effects/resolveEffect`, and Studio shows a Pending input
banner and a History tab with "Fork from here".

Other commands:

```bash
uv run nexura-runtime workflow export spec.json --out ./bundle   # standalone bundle
uv run nexura-runtime workflow run ./bundle --state '{"order_id": "ORD-1"}'
uv run nexura-studio --db ./studio.sqlite3                # older built-in Studio (nexura-studio)
```

Workflows that use your own handlers name them explicitly; workflow JSON never
chooses what code is imported:

```bash
uv run nexura-runtime workflow export spec.json --out ./bundle --handlers my_app.handlers:registry
python ./bundle/run.py '{"order_id": "ORD-1"}' --handlers my_app.handlers:registry
```

`--handlers` takes `package.module:attribute`, where the attribute is a `ModuleRegistry`
or a function that registers handlers on one. Name clashes with built-ins are rejected.

Chat turns can be streamed: `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/chat/stream` sends ordered
server-sent events for each step (model turn, tool start and finish) and ends with the
same body as the non-streaming endpoint. Reply text arrives whole (no token deltas).
A turn is saved only when it completes; if the client disconnects or stops it, nothing
is saved. The TS client exposes this as `sessions.chatStream()`.

## Package overview

**A local web page to build, run and approve `nexura-runtime` workflows, and the
`nexura-studio` command that serves it.**

```bash
pip install nexura-studio   # installs nexura-runtime, FastAPI and uvicorn too
nexura-studio --db ./studio.sqlite3   # then open http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

- **What it shows.** The available modules, saved workflows, runs with their state and
  traces, and the approval gates waiting for a person. Runs use the runtime's real
  `WorkflowEngine`; the built-in demo modules use synthetic data only.
- **This machine only.** It binds to `127.0.0.1` by default and refuses a non-loopback
  `--host` unless `NEXURA_STUDIO_TOKEN` is set (or the loudly named
  `--insecure-allow-unauthenticated-network` is passed). Every state-changing request needs
  the per-session token, which the page reads from its own origin. The token stops other
  web pages, not other programs on this machine, which can read it.
- **What stays in the runtime.** The run store, built-in modules, traces and the security
  middleware are part of `nexura-runtime` (`nexura_runtime.studio`), shared with the REST
  service. `nexura-runtime serve` (the API that the React Studio in `studio-web/` and the
  TypeScript client call) needs only `pip install "nexura-runtime[studio]"`, not this package.
- Without this package, `nexura_runtime.studio.create_app()` raises `MissingDependencyError`:
  "Nexura Studio is provided by the 'nexura-studio' package, which is not installed. Install
  it with: pip install nexura-studio".

> Status: **alpha** (0.4), Python 3.12 (the same as `nexura-runtime`). Single user, local
> use; it has not had an external security review.

## Offline example

The app is a FastAPI application, so it can be driven in-process without opening a port.

```python
import asyncio
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import httpx

from nexura_studio import create_app


async def main() -> None:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        app = create_app(db_path=Path(tmp) / "studio.sqlite3")
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(
            transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app),
            base_url="http://127.0.0.1",
            headers={"X-Nexura-Session": app.state.session_token},
        ) as client:
            modules = (await client.get("/api/v1/modules")).json()["modules"]
            print(len(modules), "modules, for example", sorted(m["name"] for m in modules)[0])
            page = await client.get("/")
            assert page.status_code == 200 and "nexura-session" in page.text


asyncio.run(main())
```

# Streaming to frontends

The runtime service offers three SSE representations on the same endpoints:

| Representation | Query | Alternative `Accept` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native Nexura (default) | `stream_format=native` | `text/event-stream` |
| AG-UI | `stream_format=ag-ui` | `application/vnd.ag-ui+json` |
| AI SDK UI messages | `stream_format=ai-sdk` | `application/vnd.vercel.ai.ui-message-stream+json` |

Use `POST /api/v1/sessions/{session_id}/chat/stream` for chat and
`GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/events?live=true` for a workflow. Request bodies,
authentication, session persistence, workspace checks and approval decisions use
the existing API. See [Service and Studio](studio-and-service.md) and
[approval gates](approvals.md). These are output adapters, not implementations of
the AG-UI `RunAgentInput` or AI SDK chat request API.

An explicit query parameter takes precedence over `Accept`. Recognized media
ranges respect `q` weights (first wins ties); `q=0` disables that range. Malformed
weights are ignored. If no recognized, acceptable range remains, the service
falls back to native, including `q=0`, malformed weights, unsupported Accept
types, absent Accept and wildcards. Invalid `stream_format` returns 400
before execution. Responses always have `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and
`Vary: Accept`. The vendor media types in this table and
`x-ag-ui-protocol-version` are **Nexura-defined selectors/metadata**, not media
types or headers specified by AG-UI or Vercel. Stock AG-UI `HttpAgent` sends
`Accept: text/event-stream`; use **`?stream_format=ag-ui`** with that client.
Protobuf (`application/vnd.ag-ui.event+proto`) is unsupported and falls back to
native; this service does not produce AG-UI protobuf. Native wire framing remains
unchanged. The output-guardrail holding rule below applies to all formats.

## Protocol pins

- **AG-UI protocol 1.0**, the lifecycle/text/tool/state/custom subset documented
  by [AG-UI events](https://docs.ag-ui.com/concepts/events). The upstream
  [core manifest](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui/blob/main/sdks/typescript/packages/core/package.json)
  identifies `@ag-ui/core` **1.0.3** and `agui.protocolVersion: "1.0"` at inspection.
  Nexura sends `x-ag-ui-protocol-version: 1.0`. It uses legacy `RUN_FINISHED`
  without `outcome`; pause meaning is carried by the custom event and
  `result.nexura.paused` below.
- **Vercel AI SDK 5.0.0**, `UIMessageChunk` SSE protocol, wire header
  **`x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1`**. Checked against the current
  [AI SDK stream documentation](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-ui/stream-protocol)
  and the immutable
  [5.0.0 chunk schema](https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/ai%405.0.0/packages/ai/src/ui-message-stream/ui-message-chunks.ts).
  Current docs describe newer SDKs too; Nexura deliberately implements this
  pinned subset. It does not use the older numeric-prefix data protocol.

No AG-UI or JavaScript SDK dependency is needed on the Python server. The adapters
were implemented from the public wire specifications; no upstream source was copied.
Verification uses local FakeModels and mock/in-process transports, not live providers
or browser SDK compatibility testing.

## AG-UI example

Send the normal Nexura chat body. Agents without output guardrails stream text
as native `TEXT_DELTA` events arrive. For an active agent with output guardrails
(its own, or a policy's contributed through hooks), the Runner itself holds the
reply (P39 G4, see [streaming and output guardrails](guardrails-hooks-limits.md#streaming-and-output-guardrails)):
with the default `stream_guard` no deltas are emitted and only guardrail-checked
`FINAL_OUTPUT` (or the saved reply) is published; with `stream_guard="chunked"`
only windows that passed every output guardrail are emitted as deltas. Rewrites
replace the unchecked answer before it is published; a tripwire publishes no
blocked text, only an error. The service forwards what the Runner emits, so the
rule applies to every format, to native Studio chat and to guarded handoff
targets. Workflow traces omit raw deltas and expose checked final output. Tool
results retain the native visibility policy; output guardrails are not a general
tool-content scrubber.

```javascript
const response = await fetch(
  '/api/v1/sessions/my-session/chat/stream?stream_format=ag-ui',
  {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'X-Nexura-Session': sessionToken, // existing local service session token
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'calculate 25 * 4' }), // local fake demo
  },
);
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);

// Feed parsed SSE data objects to your AG-UI event handler.
// Use a streaming SSE parser; a network chunk can split a frame or JSON string.
for await (const event of parseSSEData(response.body)) {
  if (event.type === 'TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT') appendText(event.messageId, event.delta);
  if (event.type === 'CUSTOM' && event.name === 'nexura.approval') showApproval(event.value);
}
```

`parseSSEData`, `appendText` and `showApproval` above are application helpers.
The output follows this shape (each `data:` line is followed by a blank line):

```text
data: {"type":"RUN_STARTED","threadId":"my-session","runId":"chat-..."}

data: {"type":"TEXT_MESSAGE_START","messageId":"chat-...:text:1","role":"assistant"}

data: {"type":"TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT","messageId":"chat-...:text:1","delta":"Hello"}

data: {"type":"TEXT_MESSAGE_END","messageId":"chat-...:text:1"}

data: {"type":"RUN_FINISHED","threadId":"my-session","runId":"chat-..."}
```

Chat uses the session ID for `threadId` and a new transport run ID per request;
the public native chat envelope does not expose the Runner's internal run ID.
Workflow `threadId` and `runId` both use the stored workflow run ID. Message and
tool IDs are scoped to the transport and to agent executions to avoid collisions.

## AI SDK example

With `ai@5.0.0`, translate the outgoing request to Nexura's chat body using
`DefaultChatTransport`. For example, in a React app using its compatible
`@ai-sdk/react` 2.x package:

```javascript
import { useChat } from '@ai-sdk/react';
import { DefaultChatTransport } from 'ai';

export function useNexuraChat(sessionToken) {
  return useChat({
    transport: new DefaultChatTransport({
      api: '/api/v1/sessions/my-session/chat/stream?stream_format=ai-sdk',
      headers: { 'X-Nexura-Session': sessionToken },
      prepareSendMessagesRequest({ messages }) {
        const last = messages[messages.length - 1];
        const message = last.parts
          .filter(part => part.type === 'text')
          .map(part => part.text).join('');
        return { body: { message } }; // server owns the persisted transcript
      },
    }),
    onData(part) {
      if (part.type === 'data-nexura-approval') showApproval(part.data);
    },
  });
}
```

Call `const chat = useNexuraChat(sessionToken)` in your component and render text
parts from `chat.messages`; dynamic tool parts contain tool names,
available input and output. `sessionToken` and `showApproval` are application
values. This output stream is also consumable using AI SDK's
`readUIMessageStream` and an SSE/`UIMessageChunk` parser. A normal completed
response ends with `finish` and `data: [DONE]`. Failures, including malformed
source frames, source exceptions and EOF without a terminal event, emit an
`error` chunk, `finish`, then `[DONE]`; exception details are withheld.
Explicit cancellation emits `data-nexura-cancelled`, `abort`, `finish`, `[DONE]`.
A client disconnect cannot receive a guaranteed terminator.

## Event mapping and approval boundaries

| Public Nexura event | AG-UI | AI SDK 5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First frame / run start | `RUN_STARTED` | `start` |
| `TEXT_DELTA` (unguarded, or a checked window) | `TEXT_MESSAGE_START/CONTENT/END` | `text-start/delta/end` |
| `FINAL_OUTPUT` without deltas for that model turn | Text message | Text part |
| `TOOL_STARTED` | `TOOL_CALL_START/ARGS/END` | `tool-input-start/delta/available` |
| `TOOL_COMPLETED` for an observed call | `TOOL_CALL_RESULT` | `tool-output-available` |
| Workflow initial/input/final state | `STATE_SNAPSHOT` | `data-nexura-state-snapshot` |
| Node `state_update` | Dropped; await next authoritative snapshot | Same |
| `RUN_PENDING_APPROVAL` / `RUN_PAUSED` | `CUSTOM: nexura.approval` | `data-nexura-approval` |
| Input/effect pause | `CUSTOM: nexura.paused` | `data-nexura-paused` |
| `GUARDRAIL_TRIPPED` after shown or chunked text | `CUSTOM: nexura.guardrail-tripped` | `data-nexura-guardrail-tripped` |
| Run success | `RUN_FINISHED` | `finish` |
| Root failure/rejection | `RUN_ERROR` | `error`, `finish` |
| Explicit cancellation | `CUSTOM: nexura.cancelled`, `RUN_FINISHED` | Cancellation data, `abort`, `finish` |

State synchronization uses snapshots only. A node's `state_update` is a raw write;
reducers such as `append` may change its meaning. Sending it as JSON Patch would
overwrite reduced state incorrectly, so it is omitted. The next node-input or
final snapshot supplies authoritative reduced state. A partial replay beginning
with a raw update waits for such a snapshot instead of inventing a baseline.
Workflow final snapshots include only the final state already present in native
SSE. Agent event wrappers (`AGENT_EVENT`) expose supported text/tool events; a
child's completion, failure or pause does not finish its parent workflow.

Approval custom payloads contain only `reason` plus any public `approval_id`,
`interrupt_id`, `effect_id` and `node_id`. **The notice** contains no arguments or
interruption transcript. Calls that later run or are refused appear as ordinary
tool events with the arguments the native stream shows. In particular, chat's
refused approval arguments can appear in `TOOL_CALL_ARGS`/`tool-input-available`.
Raw `TOOL_CALL_DELTA`, partial structured output, model
metadata, arbitrary tool custom payloads and unknown/internal events are dropped.
Only `TOOL_STARTED` arguments already visible in the native public stream can
become standard tool input events. Adapters never read the Runner, checkpoint,
approval record or database directly; existing route redaction remains authoritative.
They do not add a new general content scrubber or promise to detect arbitrary secrets
the native stream itself exposes.

A workflow pause emits its custom notice immediately. A finite replay ending at
that pause adds `RUN_FINISHED.result.nexura` with `paused: "approval"` (or
`"input"`/`"effect_unknown"`) and available public identifiers. It also retains
the custom notice. This signals the observation boundary,
**not approval or successful tool execution**. A live response retains native
polling behavior and can continue when the workflow resumes. Full replay reads
past historical pauses to later events; it does not stop at the first approval.
Use the existing approval/input/effect routes to continue execution. The chat
playground automatically refuses approval-gated tools and
continues its turn; its approval notice is informational and does not end that
chat response. Adapted chat finishes only after `chat_completed`; late response
assembly or persistence exceptions become sanitized terminal stream errors rather
than a truncated success. This guarantee applies to the adapters; native error
framing is unchanged. A disconnected chat closes its source generator and
retains the existing persistence semantics.

## Guarded replies in the native stream

The native stream is where a client sees how a guarded reply is delivered:

- The turn's `MODEL_STARTED` has `stream_guard: "hold"` or `"chunked"` when its reply is
  checked before it is shown (absent for unguarded agents). Studio shows
  "Checking reply…" in place of the live reply.
- `"hold"`: no `TEXT_DELTA`; `FINAL_OUTPUT` carries the checked reply, then
  `chat_completed` the saved one (`delivery: "final_only"`).
- `"chunked"`: `TEXT_DELTA` events with `checked: true`, each after it passed; the rest of
  the reply follows the check of the whole answer (`delivery: "streamed"`).
- A trip: `GUARDRAIL_DECISION`, then `GUARDRAIL_TRIPPED` (`stage`, `guardrail`, `agent`,
  `turn`, `phase` `"chunk"` or `"final"`, `stream_guard`, `shown`; never content), then
  `RUN_FAILED` and `chat_failed`. With `shown: true`, discard the checked windows already
  shown. The adapters close the open text message and pass this on as
  `CUSTOM` `nexura.guardrail-tripped` (AG-UI) or a transient `data-nexura-guardrail-tripped`
  part (AI SDK) with `{"discard": true|false, "phase", "stream_guard"}` when anything was
  shown or the turn was chunked, then end with their error sequence. Nothing of the blocked
  window was emitted.
- With `tool_use_behavior` that ends the run on a tool result, that call's `TOOL_COMPLETED`
  has `result_withheld: true` and no `result`: the adapters emit no tool result for it, and
  the checked answer arrives as text from `FINAL_OUTPUT`.
- Text a guarded agent writes before tool calls is checked before it is stored, so the
  transcript in `chat_completed` holds only checked text.

## Replay and stream closure

Workflow `cursor` and `Last-Event-ID` retain their native meanings. Each source
event may produce several protocol events; only its final mapped frame carries
the native SSE ID, so reconnecting after a complete group can advance the cursor.
Source events that produce no output do not advance the visible cursor. A reconnect creates
a fresh protocol envelope and fresh local text/tool state; it cannot reconstruct
an earlier partial message, unobserved tool start or missing snapshot. Use full
replay (`cursor=0`, no `Last-Event-ID`) to rebuild frontend state. This is not AI
SDK resumable-stream persistence or AG-UI thread synchronization.

A finite workflow replay, an empty replay after a cursor, or the live poll timeout
can end without a terminal run event. These emit `CUSTOM: nexura.stream-closed`
or `data-nexura-stream-closed`, with `{"terminal": false}`, followed by a terminal
protocol error (`RUN_ERROR` with `STREAM_INCOMPLETE`, or AI SDK `error`, `finish`,
`[DONE]`). The error describes an incomplete observation, not a failed workflow;
reconnect to continue observing. AG-UI always ends with `RUN_FINISHED` or
`RUN_ERROR` while connected. A finite replay ending at an approval pause is the
documented paused finish above, not an incomplete observation. Terminal runs produce exactly one terminal sequence;
duplicate native completion/stream-close frames are not forwarded.

Source: https://github.com/Liceron/nexura/blob/main/docs/remote-single-operator.md

# Run Nexura on a server (single operator)

By default `nexura-runtime serve` is for this machine only: it listens on `127.0.0.1`,
answers only loopback peers and needs no login. Remote single-operator mode lets **one
person** run the open-source service on a remote host or VM and use Studio and the REST API
over the network. One operator token protects every request.

This mode is not multi-user. Everyone who has the token is the same local owner (role
`admin`). The token carries the full authority of the operating-system user that runs the
service: whoever holds it can run workflows and the handlers registered on the host, use and
change credentials, register MCP servers and integrations, and read every run. Treat it like
that user's SSH key. Accounts, roles, SSO, organisations and per-user audit are in the Nexura
enterprise edition. A reverse proxy does not add them.

## How it works

- `nexura-runtime serve --auth token` installs the open-source `OperatorTokenAuthProvider`
  (`nexura_runtime.service.api.operator_token`) through the existing `AuthProvider` seam.
- Every HTTP and WebSocket request needs `Authorization: Bearer <operator token>`. The only
  exceptions are `/healthz` and `/readyz`. The API docs (`/docs`, `/openapi.json`) and
  extension routes need the token too.
- Webhook deliveries are the one exception to the operator token. Each webhook endpoint gets
  its own delivery token, and `POST /api/v1/triggers/webhooks/{id}/deliver` accepts only that
  token. See [Webhooks](#webhooks).
- `/readyz` returns only a status in this mode, with or without the token. Probe details are
  not served on a public route, so it cannot be used to test a guessed token. A wrong bearer
  sent to `/readyz` counts as a failed attempt; a probe that sends none is not counted.
- A missing, malformed or wrong token gets the same answer: `401` `UNAUTHENTICATED` with
  `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`. The answer does not say whether a token was sent or how close it
  was.
- After 10 failed attempts from one address within 60 seconds, that address gets `429`
  `TOO_MANY_AUTH_FAILURES` with `Retry-After` for wrong or missing tokens. The right token
  always gets through, also from a blocked address, and clears that address's failures, so
  the block never locks the operator out. For the same reason it does not limit guessing: a
  blocked address still tells a right token (200) from a wrong one (429). The block only
  marks the address and limits log noise and load. Resistance to guessing comes entirely from
  the token's randomness, so use a generated token (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`, see below):
  the server cannot measure the strength of a token a person made up.
- A request from another machine that did not arrive over HTTPS is refused with `403`
  `PLAIN_HTTP_REFUSED` before any token is read. Behind a TLS reverse proxy on the same host
  the service learns the scheme from `X-Forwarded-Proto`. `--insecure-plain-http` /
  `allow_plain_http=True` turns this off. This also covers an app that embeds
  `create_api_app()` and binds it itself.
- The service keeps only the SHA-256 hash of the token in memory and compares hashes with
  `hmac.compare_digest`. It never prints or logs the token. A rejected attempt is logged with
  the peer address and `missing` or `invalid`, never the value.
- The caller is the same local owner as on loopback. In this mode the loopback-client rule,
  the per-session `X-Nexura-Session` token and the JSON-only rule are switched off. Browsers
  never send an `Authorization` header by themselves, so another web page cannot use your
  session. Clients send only the bearer. `GET /api/v1/local-session` answers `404` to a
  signed-in client; a request to it without any bearer (an older client's probe) is refused
  but not counted as a failed attempt.

## 1. Create the token

Generate the token, do not make one up:

```bash
python -c "import secrets;print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))" > /srv/nexura/operator.token
chmod 600 /srv/nexura/operator.token
```

The token must be at least 43 characters. The server cannot measure real entropy, but it
refuses obvious non-random tokens at startup: one kind of character, a repeated piece, a long
`abcd` or `aaaa` run, words repeated, or a low estimate from character frequencies. Every
refusal prints the command above. `secrets.token_hex(32)` output is accepted too.

Give the token to the service in one of two ways, never both:

- **Prefer the token file:** `--token-file PATH` (or `NEXURA_OPERATOR_TOKEN_FILE=PATH`). The
  service opens the file once without following a symbolic link and checks that same open file
  before reading it. On Linux and macOS the file must be a regular file owned by the user that
  runs the service, with no group or other permissions (`chmod 600` or `400`); otherwise the
  service refuses to start. A UTF-8 byte-order mark and a trailing newline are ignored. On
  Windows, keep the file in a folder only you can read.
- `NEXURA_OPERATOR_TOKEN`. `nexura-runtime serve` removes the variable from its environment
  after reading it, so MCP servers and other child processes do not inherit it. The process's
  initial environment stays readable in `/proc/<pid>/environ` (and `ps eww`, `systemctl show`
  for a unit's `Environment=`) by the same user and root for as long as the service runs. Use
  the file in production. The Python API (`OperatorTokenAuthProvider.from_environment`) reads
  the variable and does not remove it. If the variable is set but `--auth token` is not given,
  `serve` prints a warning.

There is no command-line option for the token itself, because the command line shows in `ps`.
To rotate the token, write a new one and restart the service. The old token stops working at
the restart.

## 2. Start the service on loopback

Keep the service on `127.0.0.1` and let a TLS reverse proxy on the same host face the network:

```bash
nexura-runtime serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8765 \
  --db /srv/nexura/data/nexura_service.sqlite3 \
  --auth token --token-file /srv/nexura/operator.token
```

The rules:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `serve` | Loopback only, no token (unchanged default) |
| `serve --host 0.0.0.0` | Refused at startup (exit 2), as before |
| `serve --auth token` | Token required, listening on `127.0.0.1`; network requests must arrive over HTTPS (a proxy) |
| `serve --auth token --host 0.0.0.0` | Refused: the token would cross the network over plain HTTP |
| `serve --auth token --host 10.0.0.5 --insecure-plain-http` | Allowed, with a loud warning |
| `serve --auth token --insecure-allow-unauthenticated-network` | Refused: contradictory |

The service does not do TLS. Use `--insecure-plain-http` only when TLS ends somewhere else
in front of the port without setting `X-Forwarded-Proto`, such as a VPN like WireGuard or
Tailscale. In Python, the same switches are
`create_api_app(auth_provider=OperatorTokenAuthProvider(token), listen_host=...,
allow_plain_http=...)`.

A systemd unit:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Nexura service (remote single-operator mode)
After=network-online.target

[Service]
User=nexura
WorkingDirectory=/srv/nexura
ExecStart=/srv/nexura/.venv/bin/nexura-runtime serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8765 \
  --db /srv/nexura/data/nexura_service.sqlite3 --auth token \
  --token-file /srv/nexura/operator.token
Restart=on-failure
KillMode=control-group

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

## 3. Put TLS and Studio in front

The service serves the API, not the Studio files. Build Studio once
(`cd studio-web && npm ci && npm run build`) and let the proxy serve `studio-web/dist` and
forward `/api`, `/healthz` and `/readyz` to the service. Studio and the API then share one
origin. Studio calls `/api` on its own origin. The service sets no cookies and sends no CORS
headers. In this mode it accepts a browser `Origin` that equals the request's own origin
(scheme aside, its host and port must equal the `Host` header), or one listed in
`NEXURA_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`. Other origins get `403` `CROSS_ORIGIN_FORBIDDEN`.

Studio holds the operator token while a tab is open, so the proxy must send the same
Content-Security-Policy and security headers that the built-in Studio server sends
(`nexura_studio.server.STUDIO_CSP`). `connect-src 'self'` stops injected script from sending
the token to another host, and `frame-ancestors 'none'` stops other sites from framing Studio.
Both examples below set them for every response.

Caddy (`/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`) gets and renews a certificate by itself and sets
`X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `Host` for the service:

```text
nexura.example.com {
	encode gzip
	header {
		Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000"
		Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'"
		X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
		X-Frame-Options "DENY"
		Referrer-Policy "no-referrer"
	}
	request_body {
		max_size 40MB
	}
	@service path /api/* /healthz /readyz
	handle @service {
		reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8765
	}
	handle {
		root * /srv/nexura/studio-web/dist
		try_files {path} /index.html
		file_server
	}
}
```

nginx. The `add_header` lines stay in the `server` block: nginx drops them for a `location`
that has an `add_header` of its own, so do not add one to a location.

```nginx
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name nexura.example.com;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name nexura.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/nexura.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/nexura.example.com/privkey.pem;
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always;
    add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'" always;
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
    add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
    add_header Referrer-Policy "no-referrer" always;
    client_max_body_size 40m;

    root /srv/nexura/studio-web/dist;
    location / {
        try_files $uri /index.html;
    }

    location ~ ^/(api/|healthz$|readyz$) {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8765;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header Host $http_host;          # keeps the port, so Origin matches Host
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_buffering off;        # run events and chat streams are server-sent events
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
    }
}
```

`Host $http_host` passes the host and port the browser used. With `$host` the port is lost, so
on a listener other than 443 every Studio request with a body would be refused as
cross-origin. `proxy_http_version 1.1` and `proxy_buffering off` keep server-sent events
streaming.

**Trusted proxy.** `nexura-runtime serve` runs uvicorn, which takes the client address and
scheme from `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` only when the request comes from a
trusted proxy. By default only `127.0.0.1` and `::1` are trusted (uvicorn's
`FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` environment variable). With a proxy on the same host, the per-address
limit therefore counts real client addresses, and HTTPS requests are recognised. If the proxy
runs on another host, set `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` to that proxy's address. Never set it to `*`
while other machines can reach the port, because a client could then fake its address and
scheme. A proxy that forwards without `X-Forwarded-For` (a TCP passthrough, `ssh -L`) makes
every client look like `127.0.0.1`: they then share one failure count, although the right
token still always gets through.

`Host` is not restricted in this mode unless you set `NEXURA_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, for example
`NEXURA_ALLOWED_HOSTS=nexura.example.com`. Then other `Host` names get `400` `INVALID_HOST`.

## 4. Sign in

- **Studio.** Open `https://nexura.example.com`. The service refuses Studio's first request,
  so Studio shows a sign-in card. Paste the operator token. Studio sends it as
  `Authorization: Bearer` and keeps it in this tab's `sessionStorage`, so it is gone when you
  close the tab. Studio never writes the token to `localStorage`, the URL or the console. A
  token the server refuses, at sign-in or later (after a restart with a new token), is
  removed. If you change the server URL in Connection Settings to another origin, Studio drops
  the token instead of sending it there.
- **curl.** For example:
  `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.nexura-token)" https://nexura.example.com/api/v1/workflows`.
- **Python.** Use `NexuraClient("https://nexura.example.com", api_key=token)`
  (`nexura_runtime.service.api.client`).
- **TypeScript.** Use `new NexuraClient({ baseUrl: "https://nexura.example.com", apiKey: token })`.

## Webhooks

Senders never get the operator token. Each webhook endpoint has its own **delivery token**:

- Registering a webhook (`POST /api/v1/triggers/webhooks`) in this mode returns a
  `delivery_token` next to the HMAC `secret`. Both are shown once. The service keeps only the
  SHA-256 hash of the delivery token. Delivery tokens are 32 random bytes
  (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`).
- A sender calls `POST /api/v1/triggers/webhooks/{endpoint_id}/deliver` with
  `Authorization: Bearer <delivery token>` and the usual v2 HMAC signature headers
  (`X-Webhook-Signature`, `X-Webhook-Timestamp`, `X-Webhook-Event-ID`). The delivery route
  accepts only that endpoint's delivery token: not the operator token, and not another
  endpoint's token. A delivery token works on no other route.
- `POST /api/v1/triggers/webhooks/{endpoint_id}/delivery-credential` (with the operator token)
  issues a new delivery token; the old one stops working at once. Use it to rotate a token, or
  to get one for a webhook registered before remote mode was turned on (such a webhook has
  no delivery token and accepts no deliveries until you issue one). Python:
  `client.triggers.rotate_delivery_token(endpoint_id)`; TypeScript:
  `client.triggers.rotateDeliveryToken(endpointId)`. Deleting the webhook deletes its token.
- In this mode legacy v1 signatures are refused, even for an endpoint registered with
  `allow_legacy_signature=True`: v1 does not cover the event id, so a captured delivery could
  be replayed under a new id.
- Every refused delivery gets the same `401` `UNAUTHENTICATED`: an unknown or inactive
  endpoint, a wrong delivery token, a bad signature, an expired timestamp, missing or
  malformed headers and a body that is not a JSON object. The answer does not reveal which
  endpoint ids exist. Each refusal counts as a failed attempt for that address. Bodies over
  1 MB are still `413`.
- Third-party services such as Stripe, GitHub or Slack cannot deliver directly. Their
  signature schemes differ from Nexura's (they sign the raw body with their own headers), and
  they do not send a bearer token. Put a small relay in front that verifies their signature
  and re-signs the event with the Nexura scheme and the delivery token.

Studio's webhook panel shows the HMAC secret and signing snippets; in this mode the snippets'
`NEXURA_API_KEY` bearer must hold the endpoint's delivery token.

On this machine without `--auth token`, webhooks behave as before: no delivery token, the
HMAC signature alone, and only loopback senders.

## What is and is not protected

Protected:

- Every route except `/healthz` and `/readyz` needs the operator token. That includes the
  API, docs and extension routes. Webhook delivery routes need their own endpoint's delivery
  token instead.
- `/readyz` gives no details in this mode and counts wrong bearers, so it is not a token
  oracle.
- Guessing is impractical only because a generated token is 32 random bytes
  (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`). The per-address block does not limit guessing (the right
  token always passes, so a blocked address still tells right from wrong); it only limits
  log noise and load. The server rejects obvious patterns but cannot measure the strength of
  a token a person made up, so always generate it.
- The token does not appear in logs, startup output, error bodies or child-process
  environments. Existing redaction (traces, run diagnostics, repro bundles, channel text)
  already hides `Authorization` headers and values. With `NEXURA_OPERATOR_TOKEN` it stays in
  the service's own `/proc/<pid>/environ` (see above); the token file avoids that.
- Network requests over plain HTTP are refused, at startup for a non-loopback bind and at
  request time for every non-loopback peer, unless you pass `--insecure-plain-http`.

Not protected, or not provided:

- **One identity.** The token carries the service user's full authority. Nexura has no
  read-only operator, no per-person audit trail and no token expiry. Anyone who copies the
  token is you until you rotate it and restart.
- **No TLS in the service.** HTTPS is the reverse proxy's job. Over plain HTTP, a network
  observer can read the token.
- **Rate limiting is in memory and per process.** It resets on restart. It counts failed
  attempts only, not request volume. Behind a proxy it needs the trusted-proxy setting above
  to see real addresses. An address that keeps failing stays blocked for as long as it keeps
  failing; that blocks only wrong or missing tokens, never the right one, and so it is not a
  defence against guessing.
- **Studio keeps the token in `sessionStorage`.** Any script running on the Studio origin
  could read it. The CSP above limits where such script can send it; serve only the built
  Studio from that origin.
- **The rest of the security model still applies.** Workflows, handlers, MCP servers and the
  sandbox behave as in [SECURITY_MODEL.md](../SECURITY_MODEL.md). Remote access does not add
  isolation between workspaces. Local workspaces are one owner's projects.
- **Multi-user.** Several people, roles, SSO or organisations need the Nexura enterprise
  edition.

See also [Service and Studio](studio-and-service.md) for the API itself.

---

Source: https://github.com/Liceron/nexura/blob/main/docs/agents-in-studio.md

# Agents in Studio

Studio users can build their own agents and use them in workflows, the chat playground,
evaluations and red-team runs. A saved agent is a workspace resource: a declarative
`AgentSpec` (JSON, no code) stored in the service database, with a revision number.

The workflow node `nexura.agents.agent` runs a saved agent of the run's own workspace. The
older node `nexura.agents.coordinator` is unchanged; it is the offline demo (a canned support
agent that needs no model).

## The spec

Everything in a spec is a reference or text. Nothing in it is evaluated, and it cannot hold
provider strings or keys.

| Field | Meaning | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | Same rule as skill names: lowercase letters, digits, `_`, `-`; unique in the workspace | 1-64 characters |
| `description` | Short text, no control characters other than tab and newline | 500 characters |
| `instructions` | The agent's instructions | 20,000 characters |
| `model` | A name from the server's chat model allowlist (`GET /api/v1/chat/models`); default `fake-deterministic`, the offline fixture | must be configured |
| `tools` | Module ids from the app registry, exposed with `module_tool` | 20, no duplicates |
| `knowledge` | Knowledge collection ids of the workspace, searched by one `knowledge_search` tool | 10 |
| `skills` | Workspace skill names, read at `skills_label` (default `production`) when the agent runs | 20 |
| `output_schema` | Optional JSON schema for the final answer (the subset `nexura_agents` supports for dict `output_type`) | 16,000 characters; `minLength` at most 2,000 and `minItems` at most 50 |
| `limits` | `max_turns` (1-20, default 6), `max_tool_calls` (0-50, default 10), `timeout_seconds` (1-300, default 60) | |

Unknown fields are refused. The whole spec is also capped at 64,000 JSON characters.

When an agent is saved, and again every time it runs, the service checks each name against
the workspace and the server:

- the model must be in the allowlist (unknown names: `MODEL_NOT_AVAILABLE`);
- each tool must be a registered module that this workspace can see, is available on this
  server, is not flagged `internal` and is not itself an agent node. Model adapters
  (`nexura.models.*`) and modules that call a provider with a server API key (for example
  `nexura.speech`) are refused: the agent's model comes only from `model`, so a tool cannot
  choose an unlisted (paid) model or send the server's key to a URL the model picks;
- each knowledge collection and each skill must belong to the workspace; at run time the
  skills must also carry `skills_label`.

Any tool whose module can write is forced to `requires_approval=True`: a module with
`write_operations` or `always_write`, one the server gates (`approval_required_handlers`),
or any `effect_policy` other than `pure` or `read`. Its calls never run without the
approval flow.

## Routes

All under `/api/v1`. Errors are `{"detail": {"code", "message"}}`; a refused spec adds
`field_errors` (`[{"field", "message"}]`).

| Route | Role | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /agents` | viewer | Summaries (name, description, model, `tool_count`, `tools`, `approval_tools`: the tool module ids whose calls need approval, revision) plus server `limits` |
| `GET /agents/options` | viewer | Models, attachable tools (with `requires_approval`), collections, skills, limits |
| `POST /agents` | editor | Body: the spec. 201 with the record (revision 1) |
| `GET /agents/{agent_id}` | viewer | Record: `agent_id`, `revision`, `spec`, timestamps, `tools` (per-tool policy) |
| `PUT /agents/{agent_id}` | editor | Body: the spec plus `expected_revision`; 409 `REVISION_CONFLICT` (with `current_revision`) when stale; the same spec again keeps the revision |
| `DELETE /agents/{agent_id}` | admin | Optional `?expected_revision=` |

Other codes: `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` (404, also for agents of other workspaces),
`AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` (409), `TOO_MANY_AGENTS` (413, 100 agents per workspace),
`EXPECTED_REVISION_REQUIRED` (422). API keys scoped to resources cannot reach these routes.

## The agent node

Config: `agent_id` (required), `input_key` (default `input`), `output_key` (default
`output`). The node reads `state[input_key]` (text, or other JSON sent as JSON text, at most
32,000 characters), builds the agent from the spec for the run's workspace, runs it, and
writes the final answer to `state[output_key]` (the parsed object when the spec has an
`output_schema`). An `agent_id` of another workspace is not found and the node fails. The
node declares `non_idempotent_write`, so it cannot be retried.

When the agent calls a tool that needs approval, the run pauses on the normal approval path
(`status` `pending_approval` in the service, `paused` in the engine) before the call runs.
`pending_approval.details` holds `kind: "agent_tool_calls"`, the agent id, name and revision,
and the exact `calls` (`tool`, `arguments`, `digest`). Approving resumes the agent and runs
exactly those calls; rejecting ends the run and they never run. If the agent was edited in
between, the approved run fails with a message instead of running the old calls.

The pause uses two engine helpers any node can call, `request_approval(details)` and
`approved_request()` from `nexura_runtime.workflow`.

## Offline example

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from nexura_runtime.service.api.app import create_api_app

db = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "service.sqlite3"
app = create_api_app(db_path=db)  # local-owner profile, offline fixture
# Loopback base URL and peer, plus the per-session token on state-changing requests.
client = TestClient(
    app,
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1",
    client=("127.0.0.1", 50000),
    headers={"X-Nexura-Session": app.state.session_token},
)

created = client.post(
    "/api/v1/agents",
    json={"name": "greeter", "instructions": "Greet the user.", "limits": {"max_turns": 3}},
)
assert created.status_code == 201, created.text
agent = created.json()
assert agent["revision"] == 1 and agent["spec"]["model"] == "fake-deterministic"

# Use it in a workflow.
spec = {
    "name": "greet",
    "entry_node": "ask",
    "nodes": {
        "ask": {
            "id": "ask",
            "handler": "nexura.agents.agent",
            "module_id": "nexura.agents.agent",
            "config": {"agent_id": agent["agent_id"], "input_key": "q", "output_key": "a"},
        }
    },
    "terminal_nodes": ["ask"],
}
workflow_id = client.post("/api/v1/workflows", json={"spec": spec}).json()["workflow_id"]
run_id = client.post(
    "/api/v1/runs", json={"workflow_id": workflow_id, "initial_state": {"q": "hello"}}
).json()["run_id"]
run = client.get(f"/api/v1/runs/{run_id}").json()
assert run["status"] == "completed"
print(run["current_state"]["a"])  # Offline fake reply from agent 'greeter': hello

# A stale revision is refused.
stale = client.put(
    f"/api/v1/agents/{agent['agent_id']}",
    json={"name": "greeter", "instructions": "Hi!", "expected_revision": 7},
)
assert stale.status_code == 409 and stale.json()["detail"]["code"] == "REVISION_CONFLICT"
```

The offline fixture is deterministic: it echoes the input, searches knowledge for document
questions when the agent has collections, and with an `output_schema` answers with a minimal
value matching the schema (bounded to about 16,000 characters, so a recursive `$ref` stays
small). It never calls the agent's other tools.

## Write tools pause for approval

This example registers a local write module and a scripted `FakeModel` as a chat model named
`scripted`. The agent asks to create a ticket; nothing is written until a human approves.

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from nexura_agents import FakeModel
from nexura_agents.contracts.base import BaseModule
from nexura_agents.contracts.manifest import ModuleManifest
from nexura_agents.contracts.result import ModuleResult
from nexura_agents.types import ToolCall

from nexura_runtime.service.api.app import create_api_app
from nexura_runtime.workflow import ModuleRegistry

created: list[str] = []


class CreateTicket(BaseModule):
    manifest = ModuleManifest(
        module_id="demo.ticket.create",
        version="1.0.0",
        kind="integration",
        title="Create ticket",
        description="Create a support ticket.",
        input_schema={"type": "object", "properties": {"title": {"type": "string"}}},
        effect_policy="non_idempotent_write",
        always_write=True,
    )

    async def invoke(self, context, inputs, config):
        context.require_write_approval("Ticket creation")
        created.append(inputs["title"])
        return ModuleResult.success({"ticket_id": "T-1"})


def scripted(messages, tools):
    if messages[-1].role == "tool":
        return "Ticket filed."
    return [ToolCall(id="c1", name="demo_ticket_create", arguments={"title": "Printer"})]


registry = ModuleRegistry()
registry.register("demo.ticket.create", CreateTicket())
db = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "service.sqlite3"
app = create_api_app(
    registry=registry, db_path=db, chat_models={"scripted": FakeModel(handler=scripted)}
)
client = TestClient(
    app,
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1",
    client=("127.0.0.1", 50000),
    headers={"X-Nexura-Session": app.state.session_token},
)

agent = client.post(
    "/api/v1/agents",
    json={"name": "filer", "model": "scripted", "tools": ["demo.ticket.create"]},
).json()
assert agent["tools"][0]["requires_approval"] is True

spec = {
    "name": "file",
    "entry_node": "ask",
    "nodes": {
        "ask": {
            "id": "ask",
            "handler": "nexura.agents.agent",
            "module_id": "nexura.agents.agent",
            "config": {"agent_id": agent["agent_id"]},
        }
    },
    "terminal_nodes": ["ask"],
}
workflow_id = client.post("/api/v1/workflows", json={"spec": spec}).json()["workflow_id"]
run_id = client.post(
    "/api/v1/runs", json={"workflow_id": workflow_id, "initial_state": {"input": "help"}}
).json()["run_id"]
run = client.get(f"/api/v1/runs/{run_id}").json()
assert run["status"] == "pending_approval" and created == []
call = run["pending_approval"]["details"]["calls"][0]
print(call["tool"], call["arguments"])  # demo_ticket_create {'title': 'Printer'}

client.post(
    f"/api/v1/runs/{run_id}/decide",
    json={"approval_id": run["pending_approval"]["approval_id"], "decision": "approve"},
)
run = client.get(f"/api/v1/runs/{run_id}").json()
assert run["status"] == "completed" and created == ["Printer"]
print(run["current_state"]["output"])  # Ticket filed.
```

## Playground, evals and red-team

- **Chat:** `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/chat` (and `/chat/stream`) accept `agent_id`. The
  agent must be in the caller's workspace and runs on its own model, which must be in the
  allowlist; sending a different `model` is refused (`AGENT_MODEL_FIXED`) and viewers may
  use only the offline fixture. Tool calls that need approval are not run: the model is told
  they need approval, and the response lists them in `refused_tool_calls`. An agent that keeps
  asking for such tools until its turn limit gets `422 AGENT_TURN_LIMIT`. Without `agent_id`
  the playground demo is unchanged.
- **Evals:** `GET /api/v1/evaluations/studio/targets` lists saved agents as
  `{"kind": "agent", "id": "agent:<agent_id>", "version": "rev_<n>", "saved": true}`;
  `POST /evaluations/studio/runs` accepts that id. The agent runs with its real tools, so a
  call that needs approval pauses that case instead of running.
- **Red-team:** `POST /api/v1/evaluations/studio/redteam` accepts `agent_id` instead of
  `workflow_id` (exactly one). The pack uses the agent's instructions with the server's
  red-team model, exactly as for workflows: the offline fake unless the operator set
  `app.state.redteam_model`. The agent's own model is never used here (the pack sends many
  requests, and that model may be a paid one), but it must still be in the allowlist. Every
  tool that can write becomes an inert stub of the same name; other tools are not attached.

## Studio

The Studio pages use the routes above; nothing in them is evaluated, and every name,
description, instruction and argument is shown as plain text.

- **Agents page** (`#/agents`, sidebar "Agents"): the list shows each agent's model, tool count,
  revision and a "need approval" badge when any tool needs approval. The editor has name,
  description, instructions, a model select (the names from `GET /agents/options`), a tool
  checklist with a "needs approval" badge per tool, knowledge collections, skills and the
  skills label, an optional output schema as JSON text and the three limits. It checks the form
  against the server's bounds (`limits` from the options) before saving; refused fields from
  `field_errors` are shown next to the field. Saving sends `expected_revision`; a
  `REVISION_CONFLICT` shows a "Reload agent" button that loads the current revision and
  discards the unsaved edits. Viewers read only, editors create and edit, admins also delete
  (a second click confirms). The role comes from the same membership call as the Skills page.
  With no agents the page says that the model list comes from the operator
  (`NEXURA_CHAT_MODELS`) and that the offline fake (`fake-deterministic`) works without keys.
- **Workflow builder:** the node inspector of a `nexura.agents.agent` node shows a picker of the
  workspace's saved agents (name and revision) and the `input_key` and `output_key` fields
  instead of the raw config form. An `agent_id` that is not a saved agent of the workspace
  (deleted, or from another workspace) stays selected and is marked missing.
- **Approvals:** for `details.kind == "agent_tool_calls"` the approval dialog shows the agent's
  name and revision and each call's tool and arguments (indented JSON text). The `resume`
  snapshot and the call digests are never shown.
- **Playground:** an agent select sits next to the model select. With an agent chosen the turn
  sends `agent_id` and no `model`, and the model select is hidden (the agent runs on its own
  model). Tool calls in `refused_tool_calls` are listed under the transcript; a turn that ends
  with `AGENT_TURN_LIMIT` explains that tools needing approval are not run in chat.
- **Evaluations:** the run target select lists saved agents as "Saved agent: name (rev_n)". The
  Red-team tab's target select lists saved workflows and saved agents; a saved agent is sent as
  `{"agent_id": ...}` and the result shows `agent_id` and `agent_version`.

The browser test `studio-web/tests/e2e/agents.spec.ts` is written for the page, the node picker, a
workflow run and a chat with the offline model, but has not yet completed a run; component tests are in
`studio-web/tests/unit/p26_agents_studio.test.tsx`.

## Limitations

- Tools are attached with an empty module config, so modules that need config (for example
  `nexura.http.request` with `allowed_hosts`) refuse their calls.
- Agents cannot use other agent nodes as tools, and have no handoffs.
- Agent nodes cannot ask for approval inside parallel or mapped steps; the node fails there
  instead.
- The paused agent run is stored with the approval (at most 400,000 JSON characters), and a
  `request_approval` payload is capped at 512,000 characters.

---

Source: https://github.com/Liceron/nexura/blob/main/docs/local-secrets.md

# Credentials and the local encrypted secrets file

Workflows and connectors never carry a secret in their config. They name a credential
(`credential_ref`, `CredentialReference(credential_id=...)`) and the `CredentialResolver` in the
module's `ExecutionContext` resolves it inside the process, for the outbound call only. Model
providers read their own API key variables (see [Models and providers](providers.md)). This page covers where those
values come from in the open-source edition:

- **Environment-variable references.** A reference that names an `environment_variable` falls
  back to that variable when the workspace has no stored credential of that id.
- **In-memory credentials.** Without a master key, credentials created through
  `POST /api/v1/credentials` (or Studio's Credentials page) live in process memory.
- **The local encrypted secrets file.** With `NEXURA_MASTER_KEY` set, the same credentials are
  stored envelope encrypted in the service's SQLite file and survive a restart.

Organisations, the masked `/api/v1/secrets` admin API and master-key rotation are part of the
closed edition (`nexura-enterprise`, moved there in EDITIONS_PLAN step 5); the open-source
service answers 404 on `/api/v1/organisations` and `/api/v1/secrets`. Everything on this page
works without it.

## Resolving a credential

```python
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from nexura_agents.contracts import CredentialReference
from nexura_runtime.credentials import ScopedCredentialStore
from nexura_runtime.secrets import (
    EncryptedSecretStore,
    StaticMasterKeyProvider,
    generate_master_key,
)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    key = StaticMasterKeyProvider.from_text(generate_master_key())
    db = Path(tmp) / "service.sqlite3"
    store = ScopedCredentialStore(EncryptedSecretStore(key, db))
    meta = store.store("default", "github", "github_token", "ghp_example_0123456789abcdef")
    print(meta.masked_hint)  # bullets plus the last four characters
    assert b"ghp_example" not in db.read_bytes()  # encrypted at rest

    # After a restart, the same key opens the file again.
    reopened = ScopedCredentialStore(EncryptedSecretStore(key, db))
    resolver = reopened.for_workspace("default")  # a CredentialResolver for modules
    assert resolver.resolve("github") == "ghp_example_0123456789abcdef"

    # An environment-variable reference, with nothing stored under that id.
    os.environ["NEXURA_DOCS_SLACK_TOKEN"] = "xoxb-example-token-value"
    ref = CredentialReference(
        credential_id="slack",
        credential_type="slack_bot_token",
        environment_variable="NEXURA_DOCS_SLACK_TOKEN",
    )
    assert resolver.resolve(ref) == "xoxb-example-token-value"
```

`ScopedCredentialStore` always enforces workspace isolation (a reference to another
workspace is refused), revocation (a revoked credential fails closed) and redaction (a
`SecretValue` prints as `***REDACTED***`). Connectors also check the stored credential type
against the type they need. See [Connectors](connectors.md).

## The service

`create_api_app` installs the credential store once, at startup:

| Profile | `NEXURA_MASTER_KEY` | Credentials are kept |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local-owner` | unset | in memory, gone on restart |
| `local-owner` | set | encrypted in the service's SQLite file (`nexura_secrets` table, file mode 0600) |
| `authenticated-shared-service` | unset | the service refuses to start (`MasterKeyMissingError`) |
| `authenticated-shared-service` | set | encrypted in the service's SQLite file |

The only way to run the shared profile without a key is the loudly named
`NEXURA_INSECURE_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_SECRETS=I_UNDERSTAND_THIS_IS_UNSAFE` opt-out, which keeps
credentials in memory only. `app.state.secret_store` is the `EncryptedSecretStore` (or `None`)
and `app.state.credential_store` the `ScopedCredentialStore` in front of it.

Manage credentials with `GET/POST /api/v1/credentials`, `GET/DELETE /api/v1/credentials/{id}`,
`POST /api/v1/credentials/{id}/verify` and `/revoke`. Responses carry metadata and a masked
hint only, never the value. Listing and reading need the `edit` permission.

## Encryption

Each secret gets its own random 256-bit data key (AES-256-GCM). The data key is wrapped by the
master key, and both ciphertexts are bound to the workspace and the credential id, so a row
cannot be moved to another id or workspace. Starting with a different key than the one that
protects stored secrets fails closed (`MasterKeyMismatchError`); the error never contains secret
material.

Master key. `NEXURA_MASTER_KEY` holds 32 random bytes as url-safe base64; create one with
`nexura_runtime.secrets.generate_master_key()`. Key text is decoded strictly: only the url-safe
alphabet (`A-Z a-z 0-9 - _`) with optional trailing `=`, exactly 32 bytes; standard `+` and `/`,
whitespace inside the text and any other character are rejected with `MasterKeyInvalidError`,
which never echoes the text. Keep the key outside the database directory and back it up: without
it the stored credentials cannot be read.

The store uses the `cryptography` package, a core dependency of `nexura-runtime` since 0.4.0
(the `secrets` extra still exists so old install commands work, but adds nothing). If it cannot
be imported, which means a broken install, the store raises `SecretsUnavailableError`.

## Plugging in another backend

`ScopedCredentialStore(secret_store=...)` accepts any `CredentialBackend` (the protocol in
`nexura_runtime.credentials.backends`); `EncryptedSecretStore` is one. The master key is any
`MasterKeyProvider` (`key_id`, `wrap`, `unwrap`), so a key held elsewhere can wrap the data keys
instead of `NEXURA_MASTER_KEY`. See [Extending the service and Studio](extensions.md).

## Limits

There is no master-key rotation in the open-source edition. The API never returns a stored
value, so to change the key, start with the new key on a fresh database and create the
credentials again from their sources (the closed edition re-wraps them in place). No external
review has been done.
